one_line_idea: LLM tool routing in vision-agent frameworks follows tool-description semantics rather than measured tool competence: swapping two overlapping tools' natural-language descriptions redirects most calls while implementations stay fixed.
problem: Agent frameworks select vision tools by reading author-written natural-language descriptions, and nothing in the loop validates those descriptions against the tools' actual competence profiles, so routing quality is bounded by documentation quality rather than by tool quality.
core_hypothesis: The controller's routing decision is a function of description text that is largely invariant to the tools' true competence, because the loop has no channel through which execution outcomes can correct description-driven priors within or across sessions.
falsifiable_prediction: Swapping the descriptions of two partially overlapping vision tools while keeping implementations fixed will redirect at least 60% of previously routed calls to follow the swapped text. KILL: the claim dies if fewer than 30% of calls follow the swapped description, or if end-task accuracy changes by less than 1 point (meaning routing was competence-anchored or irrelevant).
why_important: Tool ecosystems scale by adding described tools; if routing never touches competence, every added tool is an unaudited failure surface and description engineering silently dominates system behavior.
why_possibly_novel: MODEL SPECULATION (unverified): prompt sensitivity of LLMs is well studied, but a controlled description-swap causal test on a fixed vision toolbox, isolating description text from tool competence at the system level, may not have been published.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Take one open agent framework with an LLM controller, two overlapping public vision tools (e.g., two captioners with different strengths), a fixed suite of 300 queries; run baseline and description-swapped conditions; measure routing-follow rate and end-task accuracy deltas.
main_risk: Well-designed toolboxes contain complementary rather than substitutable tools, making the swap condition unrepresentative of realistic routing decisions.
community_default_belief: Controllers choose sensibly among tools using descriptions as reliable competence summaries, and stronger LLMs route better.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Descriptions are written by tool authors for humans and never validated against measured competence; the controller sees only text, so it cannot outperform the text it is given.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Half a day, single GPU: one open-weight controller LLM, 100 queries, two overlapping public vision tools, one description swap; report routing-follow rate. Public data only.

one_line_idea: A tiny logistic router over cheap image/query features matches frontier-LLM tool-choice quality in vision-agent pipelines, indicating that current orchestration 'reasoning' contributes little beyond surface features.
problem: Frontier LLMs are used as tool routers on the assumption that routing requires reasoning, but the actual decision may be a shallow function of query type and coarse image statistics that a trivial model can learn.
core_hypothesis: Tool choice in typical vision-agent pipelines is predictable from a low-dimensional feature vector (query keywords, global image embedding), so replacing the LLM router with a trained shallow classifier preserves end-task accuracy at a small fraction of the cost.
falsifiable_prediction: A logistic router trained on about 1,000 routed examples will come within 2 points of the LLM router's end-task accuracy at matched tool budget. KILL: the claim dies if the LLM router beats the shallow router by more than 3 points end-task on held-out queries.
why_important: If routing is shallow, the expensive controller call per step is wasted compute for most queries, and agent-system latency and cost can drop by an order of magnitude with no accuracy loss.
why_possibly_novel: MODEL SPECULATION (unverified): distillation of full agent behavior is discussed informally, but a controlled router-substitution study isolating the routing decision (not the whole loop) may be missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Log 1,500 routing decisions from an open agent pipeline on public VQA-style data; train a logistic model on public frozen embeddings; swap it in; compare end-task accuracy and cost on a held-out split.
main_risk: Routing may be shallow on benchmark distributions but genuinely hard on rare compositional queries, so the equivalence could be an artifact of benchmark skew.
community_default_belief: Orchestration is a reasoning task that benefits from the strongest available LLM as controller.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Benchmarks contain a small number of effective query archetypes; mapping archetype to tool is a lookup, not reasoning, and the LLM's transcript is post-hoc rationalization of a shallow decision.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One day, single GPU with open-weight models and public datasets: log routings, train logistic head, measure end-task delta on 500 held-out queries.

one_line_idea: Vision-agent controllers cannot consume numeric tool metadata: decisive detector scores or OCR quality values injected into tool outputs change downstream decisions in only a small fraction of cases where they should flip the decision.
problem: Vision tools emit rich numeric metadata (detection scores, match distances, quality flags) that the loop forwards as text, but there is no evidence the controller integrates these numbers into decisions, so a designed-in information channel may be dead on arrival.
core_hypothesis: Controllers treat numeric metadata as filler text: on instances constructed so the metadata is decisive under the task rubric, decisions track the numbers far below what a rational reader would achieve, and coarse verbal quantizers (high/medium/low) outperform the raw numbers they summarize.
falsifiable_prediction: On decisive-metadata instances, controller decisions will track raw numeric scores in under 60% of cases, and replacing numbers with three-level verbal labels will raise tracking by at least 10 points. KILL: the claim dies if raw-number tracking exceeds 80%, or if verbal labels add fewer than 3 points.
why_important: Pipeline designers currently pass numbers through the interface assuming they are used; if they are not, silent failures are being shipped and a two-line quantizer wrapper is a free system upgrade.
why_possibly_novel: MODEL SPECULATION (unverified): LLM numeracy is studied in isolation, but decision-level consumption of in-context tool metadata inside multi-step vision loops may be unmeasured.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Construct 300 two-tool cases where the correct final answer flips depending on a single numeric metadata value; run an open controller with raw numbers vs verbal quantizers vs metadata removed; measure decision-tracking rates across the three interfaces.
main_risk: Constructed decisive-metadata cases may not represent natural metadata distributions, exaggerating the effect.
community_default_belief: Passing tool scores and quality values to the controller improves its decisions because the information is in context.
why_it_might_be_wrong: In-context numbers require comparison and thresholding operations that autoregressive text processing performs unreliably, so information present in context is not information used.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Half a day, single GPU, public detection/OCR outputs on public images: 100 constructed decisive cases, three interface conditions, report tracking rates.

one_line_idea: When-to-call-a-tool decisions improve more from a two-line self-probe ('answer without the tool, then estimate what the tool would add') than from scaling the controller model.
problem: Vision agents over-call tools on easy inputs and skip them on hard ones because the loop contains no explicit estimate of a tool's marginal benefit before invoking it; tool-need detection is left implicit in next-token dynamics.
core_hypothesis: Marginal-benefit estimation is latent in the controller and elicitable: forcing a draft answer plus an explicit expected-gain statement before any tool call aligns tool usage with actual marginal utility, recovering a large share of oracle-routing performance without any model change.
falsifiable_prediction: For a mid-size open controller, the self-probe recovers at least 50% of the gap between default routing and oracle routing (call the tool exactly when it changes the answer to correct) at equal or lower tool budget. KILL: the claim dies if the probe recovers under 20% of the oracle gap or increases tool calls by more than 30%.
why_important: Tool calls dominate latency and cost in deployed vision agents; a prompt-level fix that approaches oracle routing changes the economics of every tool-using system without retraining.
why_possibly_novel: MODEL SPECULATION (unverified): abstention and self-assessment are studied for final answers, but pre-call marginal-benefit elicitation as a routing mechanism inside vision loops may be untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On a public VQA-style benchmark with one high-value tool (zoom/OCR), compute oracle routing by exhaustive tool-on/tool-off evaluation, then compare default routing vs self-probe routing on accuracy and tool-call count.
main_risk: Draft answers may anchor the final response, so the probe could reduce accuracy on instances where the tool contradicts the draft.
community_default_belief: Better tool-use decisions come from stronger controllers or from fine-tuning on tool-use traces, not from prompt-level scaffolding.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The controller often already contains the knowledge of its own likely failure; the loop simply never asks for it at the decision point.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One day, single GPU: 500 public benchmark instances, exhaustive tool-on/off oracle table, two routing conditions; report oracle-gap recovery. Public data only.

evidence_label.falsifiable_prediction: EXPECTED RESULT (pre-registered threshold; no measured numbers)
evidence_label.prior_work_basis: MODEL SPECULATION: adjacent literature on selective prediction exists; pre-call marginal-benefit probes in vision loops not verified.

one_line_idea: Vision-agent answers depend on tool call order even when evidence is commutative: permuting the order of independent tool calls flips final answers at a rate comparable to swapping the controller model itself.
problem: Multi-tool queries gather evidence whose logical content is order-independent, yet the transcript is sequential, so the loop may impose an order dependence that has no epistemic justification and is invisible in standard evaluations.
core_hypothesis: Because each tool result conditions interpretation of later results in the transcript, final answers are systematically order-sensitive, and the magnitude of this order effect rivals differences attributed to controller choice.
falsifiable_prediction: On queries requiring two or more independent tool results, permuting call order flips at least 8% of final answers, and the flip rate is at least half the answer-disagreement rate between two different open controllers on the same queries. KILL: the claim dies if the order-flip rate is under 3%.
why_important: Order effects of this size mean reported agent accuracies are draws from an unmodeled distribution over execution orders, and mitigation (evidence pooling before synthesis) is cheap once the effect is established.
why_possibly_novel: MODEL SPECULATION (unverified): order sensitivity is documented for few-shot examples and multiple-choice options, but not, to my knowledge, for tool-result ordering inside vision-agent loops.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Select 300 public multi-evidence queries, run each under all orderings of 2-3 independent tool calls with fixed seeds, measure answer flip rate, and compare against a controller-swap disagreement baseline.
main_risk: Some flips may reflect genuine sampling noise rather than order; requires temperature-zero decoding and repeated-run controls.
community_default_belief: If the same evidence ends up in context, its arrival order is immaterial to the final synthesis.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Autoregressive conditioning makes early tokens causally upstream of interpretation; transcripts are not commutative evidence pools but path-dependent narratives.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Half a day, single GPU, temperature zero: 100 queries, two orderings each, report flip rate. Public data only.

evidence_label.falsifiable_prediction: EXPECTED RESULT (pre-registered threshold; no measured numbers)
evidence_label.prior_work_basis: VERIFIED PRIOR WORK (well-known): order effects for in-context examples are documented for LLMs; the tool-result ordering claim in vision loops is MODEL SPECULATION.

one_line_idea: Routing policies can improve without human labels by fine-tuning the controller on its own execution traces filtered by end-task self-consistency, because traces contain enough outcome signal to supervise tool choice.
problem: Improving tool routing currently requires human-labeled tool-use demonstrations, which do not exist for new toolboxes; the loop generates thousands of traces whose outcome statistics are discarded.
core_hypothesis: Traces where independent runs agree on the final answer are enriched for correct routing decisions, so consistency-filtered traces form a usable self-supervised dataset: a small controller LoRA-tuned on them improves routing on held-out tasks with zero human labels.
falsifiable_prediction: Trace-tuned routing closes at least 30% of the default-to-oracle routing gap on held-out task families. KILL: the claim dies if it closes under 10%, or if non-tool task accuracy drops by more than 2 points (catastrophic side effects).
why_important: Self-improving routing makes agent systems portable to new toolboxes without annotation campaigns, converting the loop from a static consumer of the controller into a training-signal generator.
why_possibly_novel: MODEL SPECULATION (unverified): self-training with consistency filters is known for reasoning chains; applying it specifically to the routing decision in vision toolchains, with routing-gap accounting, may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Generate 5,000 traces from an open 7B-class controller on public vision tasks, filter by cross-run answer agreement, LoRA-tune on the routing turns only, evaluate routing quality and end-task accuracy on held-out tasks.
main_risk: Consistency filtering enriches for easy instances, so the tuned router may improve only where routing was already trivial.
community_default_belief: Routing improvements require human demonstrations or reward models; raw traces are too noisy to learn from.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Agreement across independent runs is a strong correctness proxy precisely on the multi-step instances where routing matters, so the filter concentrates signal where it is needed.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Two days on a single GPU with open-weight models and public data: trace generation, filtering, LoRA tuning, held-out routing evaluation.

evidence_label.falsifiable_prediction: EXPECTED RESULT (pre-registered threshold; no measured numbers)
evidence_label.prior_work_basis: VERIFIED PRIOR WORK (well-known): self-consistency filtering for reasoning traces exists; routing-specific self-training in vision loops is MODEL SPECULATION.

one_line_idea: System accuracy versus toolbox size is non-monotone: pruning a vision-agent's toolbox with a held-out marginal-utility score beats the full toolbox, because overlapping tools create routing confusion that outweighs coverage gains.
problem: Toolboxes grow by accretion under the assumption that more capabilities cannot hurt, but each added tool expands the routing decision space and introduces near-duplicate options the controller must disambiguate from text alone.
core_hypothesis: There is an interior optimum in toolbox size: beyond it, marginal coverage is smaller than marginal confusion, and a simple per-tool marginal-utility estimate (accuracy with vs without the tool on a pilot set) identifies a pruned toolbox that dominates the full one.
falsifiable_prediction: For a 10+ tool vision agent, the top-half toolbox by marginal utility beats the full toolbox by at least 2 points end-task accuracy. KILL: the claim dies if the full toolbox is never worse than any utility-pruned subset across three task suites.
why_important: Toolbox curation would become a measurable engineering discipline instead of accretion, with direct accuracy and latency payoffs for every deployed agent.
why_possibly_novel: MODEL SPECULATION (unverified): choice-overload effects are known in human decision literature; a quantitative toolbox-size law with a utility-pruning recipe for vision agents may be unpublished.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Assemble a 12-tool vision agent from public tools, estimate per-tool marginal utility on 200 pilot queries, evaluate full vs pruned toolboxes on 1,000 held-out queries across three task suites.
main_risk: Marginal utility measured per-tool ignores complementarities, so pruning could remove a tool that matters only in combination.
community_default_belief: More tools mean more coverage; the controller will simply not call tools it does not need.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Routing errors scale with the number of plausible-sounding options, and description-driven routing (L-001) cannot distinguish near-duplicates, so unused tools are not harmless.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One day, single GPU, public tools and data: 12-tool agent, pilot utility estimates, full-vs-pruned comparison on 300 queries.

evidence_label.falsifiable_prediction: EXPECTED RESULT (pre-registered threshold; no measured numbers)
evidence_label.prior_work_basis: MODEL SPECULATION: no verified prior toolbox-size law for vision agents.

one_line_idea: LLM controllers are near-chance at detecting silently corrupted tool outputs, but a cheap paired-call wrapper (re-run the tool on a jittered input and compare) restores most detection without touching the controller.
problem: Vision tools fail silently — plausible captions of the wrong region, OCR of the wrong line — and the loop forwards these outputs as facts; there is no mechanism by which the controller could distinguish a confident wrong tool report from a right one.
core_hypothesis: Silent tool-failure detection is nearly impossible from a single textual report but easy from report stability: corrupted or failing tool executions are far less stable under small input jitter than healthy ones, so a compare-two-calls wrapper exposes failures the controller cannot see.
falsifiable_prediction: On injected corruptions (wrong-crop, off-by-one-region, degraded-input failures), controller-alone detection lands below 0.60 AUC while the paired-call wrapper exceeds 0.80 AUC. KILL: the claim dies if controller-alone detection reaches 0.75 AUC (wrapper unnecessary) or the wrapper stays under 0.70 (mechanism wrong).
why_important: Silent tool failure is the dominant untracked error source in tool-using vision systems; a model-agnostic wrapper that flags them changes reliability engineering for every pipeline.
why_possibly_novel: MODEL SPECULATION (unverified): input-perturbation stability is an old idea for classifiers, but using paired jittered tool calls as an in-loop failure detector for agent pipelines may be untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build a corruption-injection harness over three public vision tools inside an open agent loop; measure detection AUC for controller-prompted detection vs the paired-call stability score on 500 injected and 500 clean executions.
main_risk: Doubling tool calls doubles that component's cost, and jitter magnitude needs per-tool tuning to avoid flagging healthy-but-sensitive executions.
community_default_belief: A strong controller reading the tool output in context will notice when the output is inconsistent with the image or the task.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The controller usually cannot re-inspect the raw pixels behind the tool's report at the failure's spatial scale, so it has no independent evidence channel for verification.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One day, single GPU, public tools and images: inject 200 corruptions, compare detection AUCs of the two mechanisms.

evidence_label.falsifiable_prediction: EXPECTED RESULT (pre-registered threshold; no measured numbers)
evidence_label.prior_work_basis: MODEL SPECULATION: perturbation-stability ideas exist for classifiers; in-loop paired-call detection not verified.

one_line_idea: Auto-generated 'competence cards' — per-tool accuracy profiles measured on a small probe suite and inserted into the controller prompt — improve routing more than hand-written tool descriptions.
problem: The controller's only knowledge of a tool is its author-written description, which encodes intent rather than measured behavior; the description-competence gap (which conditions the tool fails on) is exactly what routing needs and exactly what descriptions omit.
core_hypothesis: A standardized probe suite run once per tool yields a compact empirical competence card (strong on X, fails on Y-type inputs), and conditioning the controller on cards instead of descriptions moves routing toward competence-anchored decisions measurably.
falsifiable_prediction: Competence cards close at least 40% of the default-to-oracle routing gap, beating improved hand-written descriptions on the same toolbox. KILL: the claim dies if cards close under 10% of the gap or fail to beat hand-written descriptions.
why_important: Cards make tool onboarding empirical and self-serve: any new tool gets probed and described by measurement, breaking the dependence of system quality on documentation quality identified in the description-swap line of work.
why_possibly_novel: MODEL SPECULATION (unverified): model cards exist as documentation practice, but machine-generated, probe-measured competence summaries consumed by a routing LLM inside a vision loop may be untested as a mechanism.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Define a 100-item probe suite spanning input conditions; generate cards for 8 public tools; compare routing quality under description vs card prompts against an exhaustive-evaluation oracle on 500 held-out queries.
main_risk: Cards compress competence into text the controller may again fail to consume (see the metadata-consumption problem), requiring careful verbal formatting.
community_default_belief: Better routing comes from better controllers; tool documentation is a fixed input, not a design surface.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Routing is bounded by the information in the prompt about tool behavior; enriching that information attacks the binding constraint directly.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One day, single GPU: probe 4 public tools, build cards, run 200 held-out queries under both prompt conditions. Public data only.

evidence_label.falsifiable_prediction: EXPECTED RESULT (pre-registered threshold; no measured numbers)
evidence_label.prior_work_basis: MODEL SPECULATION: model-card documentation practice is real; probe-measured cards as routing inputs not verified.

one_line_idea: Orchestration prompts and routing policies tuned on one controller LLM transfer poorly to another: the cross-controller transfer penalty exceeds the tuning gain itself, making agent-framework results controller-specific claims.
problem: Agent frameworks publish scaffold designs (prompts, tool schemas, loop structure) as if they were controller-independent artifacts, but every design decision was co-adapted to one controller's quirks during development.
core_hypothesis: Scaffold tuning is controller-specific adaptation: most of the gain from tuning a vision-agent scaffold on controller A disappears or reverses when the scaffold is run with controller B, so scaffold and controller form a coupled system that must be evaluated jointly.
falsifiable_prediction: Across two open controllers, less than 40% of scaffold-tuning gain survives a controller swap on average. KILL: the claim dies if 70% or more of the tuning gain survives the swap in both directions.
why_important: If scaffolds do not transfer, the field's practice of comparing frameworks across papers (each tuned on different controllers) confounds scaffold quality with co-adaptation, and practitioners inherit silent regressions when they swap models.
why_possibly_novel: MODEL SPECULATION (unverified): prompt-transfer brittleness is known anecdotally; quantifying scaffold-level transfer for multi-step vision agents with gain-survival accounting may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Tune a vision-agent scaffold (prompt wording, report formats, loop depth) on controller A via 20 iterations of pilot feedback; measure gains on A and on untouched controller B across three task suites; repeat in the B-to-A direction.
main_risk: Tuning quality is experimenter-dependent; weak tuning would show trivially poor transfer without testing the co-adaptation claim.
community_default_belief: A well-designed agent scaffold is a modular artifact that improves any sufficiently strong controller.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Scaffold tuning fits the idiosyncratic failure surface of one model (its parsing habits, report format preferences, tool-name biases), which is exactly what differs across model families.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One day, single GPU, two open-weight controllers, public data: 10 tuning iterations on A, transfer measurement on B, 300 queries per condition.

evidence_label.falsifiable_prediction: EXPECTED RESULT (pre-registered threshold; no measured numbers)
evidence_label.prior_work_basis: MODEL SPECULATION: anecdotal prompt-brittleness reports exist; scaffold-level transfer accounting not verified.

family_fingerprint.manipulated_variable: controller swap under fixed tuned scaffold

one_line_idea: The text interface between vision tools and the controller imposes a measurable information ceiling: a probe trained to answer spatial questions from the loop's textual intermediates plateaus far below one trained on the tool's raw outputs.
problem: Every vision-agent loop compresses tool outputs into text before the controller reasons over them, but the field has no measurement of how much task-relevant information that compression destroys, so interface design is guesswork.
core_hypothesis: For spatially structured tasks, the verbalization step is the binding constraint: the achievable accuracy from textual intermediates is capped well below the accuracy achievable from the raw tool outputs they summarize, independent of controller strength.
falsifiable_prediction: A trained probe answering spatial-relation questions from textual intermediates will trail a matched probe using raw tool outputs by at least 10 accuracy points. KILL: the claim dies if the gap is under 3 points (interface loss negligible).
why_important: If the interface, not the controller, caps system performance, the field's investment in bigger controllers is misallocated and interface engineering becomes the highest-leverage lever.
why_possibly_novel: MODEL SPECULATION (unverified): information-bottleneck framings exist in representation learning, but a direct probe-based measurement of text-interface loss in agent loops may be missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Freeze one detector-style tool and its verbalizer inside an open agent loop; train two small probes (one on textual intermediates, one on raw structured outputs) to answer the same spatial questions; compare plateaus at matched probe capacity and data.
main_risk: Probe capacity and training-data size confound the comparison; both conditions need matched budgets and convergence checks.
community_default_belief: Text is a sufficient universal interface; a good verbalizer preserves what matters and stronger controllers compensate for any residual loss.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Spatial structure (precise extents, relative geometry, dense layouts) is exactly what natural-language summaries drop first, and no controller can recover information the interface destroyed.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One day, single GPU: 5,000 auto-generated spatial QA pairs on public images, two probes, plateau comparison. Public data only.

evidence_label.falsifiable_prediction: EXPECTED RESULT (pre-registered threshold; no measured numbers)
evidence_label.prior_work_basis: MODEL SPECULATION: information-bottleneck theory exists; probe-based interface-loss measurement in agent loops not verified.

family_fingerprint.manipulated_variable: interface representation (text vs raw tool output)

one_line_idea: Agent loops that pass localization results as numeric coordinates lose to loops that render the same results as visual marks on the image: the interface encoding, not the information content, drives the gap.
problem: Localization tools return coordinates, and most agent loops forward them as JSON text, implicitly assuming the controller can do coordinate arithmetic; mark-based prompting suggests otherwise but no controlled same-information comparison inside multi-step loops exists.
core_hypothesis: Holding the information content fixed, encoding localization results as rendered marks outperforms coordinate text because the controller's spatial reasoning operates on visual tokens, not on numeric literals; the deficit grows with object count and with the number of loop steps the coordinates must survive.
falsifiable_prediction: At identical tool outputs, the mark-rendered interface beats the coordinate-JSON interface by at least 5 points on multi-object spatial tasks, with the gap growing monotonically in object count. KILL: the claim dies if the gap is under 2 points or does not grow with object count.
why_important: This isolates a design law for every loop that moves spatial data: render, don't recite — with direct implications for tool API design across frameworks.
why_possibly_novel: MODEL SPECULATION (unverified): mark-based visual prompting is established as a technique; the controlled information-equivalent encoding comparison inside multi-step loops, and its scaling with steps and objects, may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Fix a localization tool's outputs on public images; build two interface conditions (JSON coordinates vs rendered numbered marks); evaluate the same controller on spatial-relation and selection tasks stratified by object count and loop depth.
main_risk: Rendering marks consumes image-token budget and can occlude content, so gains may reverse on cluttered scenes.
community_default_belief: Structured coordinate output is the clean, lossless way to pass localization between components; visualization is a UI nicety.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Numeric coordinates in text require arithmetic the controller performs unreliably, while marks convert the problem back into perception, which is what the model is good at.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Half a day, single GPU: 300 stratified spatial queries on public images, two encodings, report the gap by object-count bin.

evidence_label.community_default_belief: MODEL SPECULATION (inferred from API design norms)
evidence_label.falsifiable_prediction: EXPECTED RESULT (pre-registered threshold; no measured numbers)
evidence_label.prior_work_basis: VERIFIED PRIOR WORK (well-known): set-of-mark visual prompting exists; the information-controlled loop-level comparison is MODEL SPECULATION.

family_fingerprint.measurement_family: spatial-task accuracy gap by object count

one_line_idea: Prose tool reports cause downstream attribute hallucination: a traceable share of final-answer errors originates at the verbalization step rather than in the vision tool or the controller's reasoning, and structured key-value reports cut this error class.
problem: Verbalizers that turn tool outputs into fluent prose add connective tissue — articles, adjectives, spatial phrases — that was never in the tool output; the loop then treats these additions as observations, but no error accounting attributes final mistakes to this step.
core_hypothesis: Verbalization is an active error source, not a neutral channel: fluent prose reports inject unsupported attributes at a measurable rate, these injections propagate to final answers, and replacing prose with minimal key-value reports removes the injected-attribute error class without losing task-relevant content.
falsifiable_prediction: Step-level ablation will attribute at least 30% of attribute-type final errors to the verbalization step, and key-value reports will cut those errors by at least half. KILL: the claim dies if under 10% of attribute errors trace to verbalization.
why_important: Error attribution across loop stages is the precondition for fixing agent systems; showing a large, removable interface-born error class redirects debugging effort from models to formats.
why_possibly_novel: MODEL SPECULATION (unverified): hallucination is studied at the model level; stage-attributed hallucination accounting inside tool loops, with a format-level fix, may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Instrument an open agent loop to log tool-raw, verbalized, and final stages; on public VQA-style data, diff injected attributes between stages; rerun with key-value reports and compare attribute-error rates.
main_risk: Attribute diffing needs a reliable extractor; noisy extraction could over- or under-attribute the interface's contribution.
community_default_belief: Hallucination lives in the VLM or the controller; the verbalization of tool outputs is a faithful formatting step.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Fluency objectives reward plausible elaboration, so the verbalizer is structurally incentivized to say more than the tool measured.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One day, single GPU: 300 instances, three-stage logging, attribute diffing with an open extractor, prose vs key-value comparison. Public data only.

evidence_label.community_default_belief: MODEL SPECULATION (inferred from model-centric hallucination framing)
evidence_label.falsifiable_prediction: EXPECTED RESULT (pre-registered threshold; no measured numbers)
evidence_label.prior_work_basis: MODEL SPECULATION: hallucination literature exists at model level; stage-attributed loop accounting not verified.

one_line_idea: Information loss across chained text handoffs compounds superlinearly: two verbalization steps lose more than twice one step's information, because each step re-summarizes an already-lossy summary.
problem: Deep agent pipelines relay visual information through multiple text handoffs (tool to sub-agent to controller), and designers implicitly assume losses add; if they compound, deep pipelines are structurally worse than their per-step audits suggest.
core_hypothesis: Each verbalization step drops details that later steps would have needed to summarize faithfully, so the second hop degrades disproportionately: relay loss grows superlinearly with hop count, and the compounding factor is stable enough to characterize as an interface law.
falsifiable_prediction: The accuracy drop from a 2-hop text relay exceeds twice the 1-hop drop by at least 50% relative on detail-sensitive tasks. KILL: the claim dies if 2-hop loss is within 20% of additive (compounding negligible).
why_important: A compounding law would set a hard depth budget for text-mediated pipelines and quantify exactly when latent or visual handoffs become necessary.
why_possibly_novel: MODEL SPECULATION (unverified): the telephone-game intuition is folklore; measured compounding curves for visual-information relays in agent systems may not exist.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Construct relay chains of depth 0-3 over fixed images with a fixed final question set; each hop re-describes the previous hop's text plus no image access; measure accuracy vs depth and fit the compounding curve.
main_risk: Compounding may be dominated by one weak verbalizer rather than being a general interface property; needs multiple verbalizer models.
community_default_belief: Per-hop losses are roughly independent and additive; a two-stage pipeline with two good summarizers is about as good as the sum of its parts.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Summarizing a summary is a different, harder task than summarizing an observation: the second hop inherits ambiguity without access to ground truth, multiplying rather than adding error.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Half a day, single GPU: 200 images, depth 0-2 relays with one open verbalizer, accuracy-vs-depth curve. Public data only.

evidence_label.community_default_belief: MODEL SPECULATION (inferred from modular-pipeline design norms)
evidence_label.falsifiable_prediction: EXPECTED RESULT (pre-registered threshold; no measured numbers)
evidence_label.prior_work_basis: MODEL SPECULATION: no verified prior measurement of relay compounding in vision-agent pipelines.

one_line_idea: Replacing the text handoff between a vision tool and the controller with a small learned adapter that injects continuous tokens recovers most of the interface-lost accuracy, isolating discretization — not controller reasoning — as the binding constraint.
problem: If the text interface destroys task-relevant visual information (the interface-ceiling hypothesis), the constructive question is whether a minimal latent channel recovers it without redesigning either the tool or the controller.
core_hypothesis: A lightweight adapter mapping tool feature vectors to a few soft tokens in the controller's embedding space preserves the spatial detail text drops; the recovery it achieves directly measures how much of the loop's failure was interface discretization rather than reasoning capacity. This is an architecture change justified by a specific mechanism claim: the loss is located at the discretization step.
falsifiable_prediction: The latent handoff recovers at least 60% of the measured text-vs-raw probe gap on spatial tasks at unchanged controller weights. KILL: the claim dies if recovery is under 25% (loss is not primarily discretization) or if an equally sized text-augmentation (longer, structured reports) matches the latent channel.
why_important: This turns the interface-bottleneck diagnosis into a deployable fix and provides the field a causal decomposition of loop failures into interface vs reasoning components.
why_possibly_novel: MODEL SPECULATION (unverified): soft-prompt and adapter methods are standard for end-to-end multimodal training; using a frozen-controller adapter specifically as an interface-loss meter inside tool loops may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train a two-layer adapter from a frozen public detector's features to 8 soft tokens of a frozen open controller using auto-generated spatial QA; compare text-interface, latent-interface, and raw-oracle conditions on held-out questions.
main_risk: Adapter training data may leak task specifics, flattering the latent channel; requires disjoint question generators for train and test.
community_default_belief: Fixing agent loops means better prompts or bigger controllers; the text interface is a fixed, adequate substrate.
why_it_might_be_wrong: No prompt can carry information the verbalizer already destroyed; only widening the channel can, and a few soft tokens are enough to test that.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Two days, single GPU, open-weight models, public images: adapter training plus three-condition evaluation on 2,000 held-out questions.

evidence_label.falsifiable_prediction: EXPECTED RESULT (pre-registered threshold; no measured numbers)
evidence_label.prior_work_basis: VERIFIED PRIOR WORK (well-known): adapter/soft-prompt methods exist; their use as an interface-loss meter in tool loops is MODEL SPECULATION.

family_fingerprint.manipulated_variable: handoff medium (text vs learned soft tokens)

one_line_idea: Making tool reports question-aware — forwarding the user question to the tool's report generator — beats upgrading to a larger controller, because relevance filtering at the interface dominates reasoning capacity downstream.
problem: Tools inside agent loops report generically because they never see the question; the controller then reasons over reports optimized for no task in particular, wasting the interface's limited bandwidth on irrelevant detail.
core_hypothesis: The single highest-leverage bit of context at the interface is the question itself: question-conditioned reports allocate the text channel to task-relevant content, and this interface fix yields larger end-task gains than swapping in a controller one size class larger.
falsifiable_prediction: Question-aware reports gain at least 4 points end-task over question-agnostic reports with the same controller, exceeding the gain from a one-class-larger controller with agnostic reports. KILL: the claim dies if question-awareness gains under 1 point or the larger controller dominates it.
why_important: It reorders the field's upgrade path: before buying a bigger controller, thread the question through the interface — a zero-training change to loop wiring.
why_possibly_novel: MODEL SPECULATION (unverified): question-conditioned captioning exists as a task; a controlled comparison of interface-conditioning vs controller-scaling inside tool loops may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: In an open loop with a captioner-style reporting tool, run four cells (agnostic/aware reports x small/large controller) on public compositional questions; compare marginal gains of the two interventions.
main_risk: Question-aware reporting can overfit the report to a misread question, hurting cases where the controller would have re-interpreted correctly.
community_default_belief: Component quality and controller scale drive system quality; report content is a minor plumbing detail.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The interface is a narrow channel; what crosses it matters more than how much intelligence waits on the far side.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Half a day, single GPU: 300 questions, 2x2 design with open-weight models. Public data only.

evidence_label.falsifiable_prediction: EXPECTED RESULT (pre-registered threshold; no measured numbers)
evidence_label.prior_work_basis: MODEL SPECULATION: question-conditioned captioning exists as a task; the interface-vs-scale tradeoff measurement is unverified.

family_fingerprint.manipulated_variable: question-conditioning of reports vs controller scale

one_line_idea: Referring-expression drift is a loop failure, not a VLM failure: multi-turn agents lose object identity as similar-object count grows, and assigning persistent visual IDs (numbered marks) at first sight eliminates most identity errors without changing any model.
problem: Agents refer to objects across turns with natural-language descriptions ('the second dog from the left'), which decay as context grows and viewpoints shift; identity errors then masquerade as perception errors in evaluations.
core_hypothesis: Identity maintenance through descriptive text is the failure mechanism: identity-error rate rises with the count of similar distractors and with turns elapsed since first mention, and a persistent numbered-mark scheme (stamp IDs at first detection, reuse everywhere) removes the text-decay pathway.
falsifiable_prediction: Identity-error rate grows monotonically with distractor count, and persistent marks cut it by at least 50% relative. KILL: the claim dies if marks help less than 15% relative (identity loss is not interface-borne) or if error shows no distractor-count dependence.
why_important: Long-horizon visual agents (inspection, retail, robotics video QA) live or die on identity tracking; a model-free wiring fix that halves identity errors is immediately deployable.
why_possibly_novel: MODEL SPECULATION (unverified): visual marks are used for single-turn grounding; persistent cross-turn identity marking as a loop-state mechanism, with drift accounting, may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build multi-turn tasks over public multi-object images (track, compare, and re-query specific instances across 5+ turns); measure identity errors vs distractor count with and without persistent marks under a fixed controller.
main_risk: Mark clutter on dense scenes may trade identity errors for perception errors; needs a density-stratified analysis.
community_default_belief: Identity errors reflect weak VLM grounding and will fall as models improve.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The same VLM that fails identity across turns succeeds within one turn; what breaks is the textual reference chain the loop forces between turns.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One day, single GPU: 200 multi-turn episodes on public images, marks on/off, identity-error rates by distractor bin.

evidence_label.community_default_belief: MODEL SPECULATION (inferred from model-centric error framing)
evidence_label.falsifiable_prediction: EXPECTED RESULT (pre-registered threshold; no measured numbers)
evidence_label.prior_work_basis: VERIFIED PRIOR WORK (well-known): mark-based grounding exists for single turns; persistent cross-turn ID marking is MODEL SPECULATION.

one_line_idea: Agent pipelines exhibit round-number bias in quantitative visual estimates that single-pass VLMs do not: repeated verbalization quantizes sizes, counts, and distances toward salient round values, and the bias grows with loop depth.
problem: Quantitative visual estimates (how many, how large, how far) pass through multiple text restatements inside loops; each restatement is an opportunity for rounding, and the aggregate effect on the output distribution is uncharacterized.
core_hypothesis: Verbalization steps act as attractors toward round and culturally salient numbers; the excess mass at round values grows with the number of restatements, making loop depth a causal variable for quantitative bias independent of the underlying VLM's perception.
falsifiable_prediction: Round-number excess mass in loop outputs will exceed single-pass outputs by at least a factor of 2 on continuous estimation tasks, and will increase monotonically over 1-3 restatement hops. KILL: the claim dies if loop and single-pass output distributions are statistically indistinguishable in round-number mass.
why_important: Downstream consumers (measurement, inventory, safety monitoring) treat agent numbers as estimates with noise, not with structured quantization artifacts; a depth-dependent bias law changes how such outputs must be post-processed.
why_possibly_novel: MODEL SPECULATION (unverified): round-number preference is documented in human forecasting; its emergence and compounding inside multi-step agent pipelines may be unmeasured.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Generate estimation tasks with known continuous ground truth from procedurally rendered public scenes; run single-pass and depth-1..3 relay pipelines; compare output histograms for round-value excess and depth trends.
main_risk: The base VLM may itself have round-number bias large enough to mask the loop's marginal contribution; needs the depth-0 baseline subtraction.
community_default_belief: Loop depth affects cost and maybe accuracy, but the error distribution's shape is a property of the perception model.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Language is a quantizing medium: every restatement re-samples from a distribution peaked at nameable values, an effect that has nothing to do with perception quality.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Half a day, single GPU: 500 rendered estimation items, depth 0-2, histogram comparison. Public/procedural data only.

evidence_label.falsifiable_prediction: EXPECTED RESULT (pre-registered threshold; no measured numbers)
evidence_label.prior_work_basis: MODEL SPECULATION: human round-number bias is documented; loop-induced quantization not verified.

family_fingerprint.measurement_family: round-number excess mass in output distribution

one_line_idea: For multi-step visual tasks, storing history as image crops beats storing text summaries at matched context budget: text memory, not context length, is the binding constraint on long-horizon visual agents.
problem: Agent frameworks summarize visual history into text to save context, assuming the summary preserves what later steps need; but later steps' needs are unknown at summarization time, and visual details are the first casualties.
core_hypothesis: Deferring interpretation preserves option value: raw crop memory lets the agent re-extract whatever a later question needs, while text memory commits early to one interpretation; at equal token budgets, crop memory wins on tasks whose later steps depend on earlier visual detail.
falsifiable_prediction: Crop-memory agents beat text-memory agents by at least 5 points on recall-of-earlier-detail tasks at matched context budget. KILL: the claim dies if the gap is 1 point or less, or if text memory wins at every budget.
why_important: Memory design is a first-class choice in every long-horizon agent; establishing the visual-vs-text memory law redirects framework defaults and context-budget allocation.
why_possibly_novel: MODEL SPECULATION (unverified): retrieval-augmented memory is standard for text agents; a controlled crop-vs-summary memory comparison at matched budgets for visual agents may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build 10+ step episodes over public image sets where step k queries details seen at step k-5 or earlier; run identical controllers with crop memory vs summary memory at three matched budgets; compare recall-dependent accuracy.
main_risk: Crop selection policy confounds the comparison: bad crops lose to good summaries, so the crop policy must be simple and fixed.
community_default_belief: Text summaries are the efficient memory medium; keeping pixels around is wasteful when context is scarce.
why_it_might_be_wrong: A summary answers yesterday's question; a crop answers tomorrow's. Option value dominates compression efficiency when future queries are unpredictable.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One day, single GPU: 100 episodes, two memory types, one budget, recall-task accuracy. Public data only.

evidence_label.falsifiable_prediction: EXPECTED RESULT (pre-registered threshold; no measured numbers)
evidence_label.prior_work_basis: MODEL SPECULATION: text-agent memory literature exists; matched-budget visual memory comparison not verified.

one_line_idea: A task-agnostic 'interface bandwidth' score — measured by freezing tools and controller and swapping only the interface encoding — predicts which task families an agent framework will fail on before any end-to-end evaluation.
problem: Agent frameworks are compared end-to-end, task by task, which is expensive and uninformative about why one framework loses; there is no standard instrument that measures the interface itself.
core_hypothesis: Frameworks differ primarily in how much task-relevant information their interfaces transmit; a bandwidth score computed from a small battery of information-recovery probes (spatial, attribute, identity, quantity) rank-predicts end-task performance across task families better than controller identity does.
falsifiable_prediction: The bandwidth score rank-correlates with end-task accuracy across at least 6 task families at Spearman rho of at least 0.6, and beats controller-size ranking as a predictor. KILL: the claim dies if rho falls below 0.3 (interface not predictive).
why_important: A cheap, standardized interface meter converts agent-framework comparison from anecdote into measurement and gives designers a target metric that is causally upstream of task performance.
why_possibly_novel: MODEL SPECULATION (unverified): benchmark suites for agents exist at the task level; a component-level interface instrument with predictive-validity claims may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Define 4 probe batteries; compute bandwidth scores for 4 open frameworks under a fixed controller and toolset; evaluate all frameworks on 6 public task families; test rank prediction against the score and against controller-scale baselines.
main_risk: Probe batteries may accidentally encode task-family content, making prediction circular; batteries must be built from disjoint data.
community_default_belief: End-to-end task benchmarks are the only meaningful comparison for agent systems; component metrics do not transfer.
why_it_might_be_wrong: When one component (the interface) is the binding constraint, measuring it directly predicts the whole system, the same way memory bandwidth predicts throughput for memory-bound programs.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One day, single GPU: 2 frameworks, 4 probes, 3 task families; check preliminary rank agreement. Public data only.

evidence_label.falsifiable_prediction: EXPECTED RESULT (pre-registered threshold; no measured numbers)
evidence_label.prior_work_basis: MODEL SPECULATION: agent benchmarks exist; component-level interface instruments not verified.

family_fingerprint.manipulated_variable: interface encoding swap under frozen components
family_fingerprint.measurement_family: rank correlation of bandwidth score with end-task accuracy

one_line_idea: Self-consistency voting saturates almost immediately for perception-bound questions because samples share the same wrong percept: the accuracy-vs-samples curve flattens by k=4 while reasoning-bound questions keep climbing.
problem: Test-time sampling-and-voting is imported from math/reasoning into multimodal systems on the assumption that more samples find the right answer, but perceptual errors may be deterministic properties of the encode, not sampling noise.
core_hypothesis: For questions whose difficulty lies in perception, error is locked in at encoding: resampled generations vary in wording but share the percept, so vote diversity is fake and gains saturate at tiny k, unlike reasoning-bound questions where paths genuinely diverge.
falsifiable_prediction: On perception-bound splits, accuracy gain from k=4 to k=32 samples is under 1 point, while matched reasoning-bound splits gain at least 3 points over the same range. KILL: the claim dies if perception-bound splits gain 2+ points from k=4 to k=32.
why_important: Test-time compute budgets are being allocated to sampling by default; if perception saturates at k=4, most of that spend is provably wasted and should move to re-encoding strategies.
why_possibly_novel: MODEL SPECULATION (unverified): self-consistency is established for reasoning; a perception-vs-reasoning stratified saturation law with an error-correlation mechanism may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Stratify a public multimodal benchmark into perception-bound and reasoning-bound splits via human or rubric tagging; run one open VLM at k in {1,4,8,16,32}; plot both curves and compare inter-sample answer entropy.
main_risk: The stratification itself is contestable; needs two independent tagging methods to show the split is robust.
community_default_belief: More samples plus voting reliably buys accuracy across task types; test-time compute is fungible.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Sampling randomizes the decoder, not the encoder: if the percept is wrong, every sample inherits it, so votes are correlated and majority voting converges on the shared mistake.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Half a day, single GPU: 300 tagged questions, k sweep with one open VLM, two curves. Public data only.

evidence_label.falsifiable_prediction: EXPECTED RESULT (pre-registered threshold; no measured numbers)
evidence_label.prior_work_basis: VERIFIED PRIOR WORK (well-known): self-consistency voting for reasoning exists; the perception-saturation law is MODEL SPECULATION.

family_fingerprint.manipulated_variable: sample count k by question type

one_line_idea: Longer reasoning chains between looking and answering degrade fine-grained visual accuracy: forced chain length causally increases detail errors, indicating that verbal reasoning overwrites visual detail in the loop's working state.
problem: Chain-of-thought is applied uniformly to multimodal questions, but the tokens generated between image encoding and answer emission may function as interference for fine-grained visual information rather than as useful computation.
core_hypothesis: Visual detail available at answer time decays with the number of intervening generated tokens: forcing longer chains (padding with topically relevant but non-informative reasoning) causally lowers accuracy on detail-critical questions, with a monotone dose-response.
falsifiable_prediction: Forcing an extra 200 reasoning tokens reduces fine-detail accuracy by at least 3 points with a monotone trend across 0/100/200/400 forced tokens. KILL: the claim dies if the effect is 1 point or less, or non-monotone across the dose sweep.
why_important: If reasoning length is a perception tax, chain policies must become question-type-conditional, and 'think more' stops being a safe default for multimodal systems.
why_possibly_novel: MODEL SPECULATION (unverified): reports that chain-of-thought sometimes hurts perception exist informally; a controlled dose-response with content-controlled padding may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On detail-critical public questions (small text, thin structures, subtle attributes), force chains of controlled lengths via instructed padding; measure accuracy vs dose with fixed decoding and matched final-answer formats.
main_risk: Padding content may itself mislead semantically; padding must be validated as answer-neutral in a no-image control.
community_default_belief: More explicit reasoning cannot hurt and usually helps; length is a free parameter to scale.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Attention over a growing text prefix competes with fixed visual tokens; each generated token dilutes the visual signal available to the answer head.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Half a day, single GPU: 300 detail questions, 3 dose levels, one open VLM. Public data only.

evidence_label.falsifiable_prediction: EXPECTED RESULT (pre-registered threshold; no measured numbers)
evidence_label.prior_work_basis: VERIFIED PRIOR WORK (well-known): chain-of-thought prompting exists; the dose-response interference claim is MODEL SPECULATION.

one_line_idea: For perception-bound tasks, spending test-time compute on re-looking (fresh encodes of question-relevant crops) dominates spending it on re-thinking (more reasoning tokens) at every matched budget point.
problem: Test-time compute can buy tokens or buy pixels, but the field lacks an exchange rate: no controlled comparison holds FLOPs fixed while varying the split between additional reasoning and additional visual encoding.
core_hypothesis: Perception-bound accuracy is limited by what was encoded, so marginal compute converts to accuracy at a higher rate through re-encoding question-relevant crops than through generating more reasoning tokens; the re-look curve dominates the re-think curve across budgets.
falsifiable_prediction: At three matched compute budgets, the re-look allocation beats the re-think allocation on perception-bound tasks at every point, with a gap of at least 3 points at the middle budget. KILL: the claim dies if re-think matches or beats re-look at most budget points.
why_important: An empirical exchange rate between tokens and pixels gives every system builder a principled allocation rule for inference budgets, replacing the current default of scaling text.
why_possibly_novel: MODEL SPECULATION (unverified): zoom/crop pipelines and long-chain reasoning exist separately; an iso-FLOP allocation frontier between them may be unmeasured.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Fix an open VLM; define budget points in encoder+decoder FLOPs; implement re-look (grid or question-guided crops re-encoded) and re-think (longer chains, more samples) allocations; sweep on perception-bound public tasks.
main_risk: FLOP accounting across encoder and decoder is architecture-specific and must be published with the harness to be credible.
community_default_belief: Test-time scaling means longer chains and more samples; visual re-encoding is an implementation detail rather than a compute-allocation choice.
why_it_might_be_wrong: You cannot reason your way to a pixel you never encoded; for perception-bound questions the informative marginal compute is in the encoder.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One day, single GPU: one budget point, both allocations, 300 perception-bound questions. Public data only.

evidence_label.community_default_belief: MODEL SPECULATION (inferred from text-centric scaling practice)
evidence_label.falsifiable_prediction: EXPECTED RESULT (pre-registered threshold; no measured numbers)
evidence_label.prior_work_basis: MODEL SPECULATION: no verified iso-FLOP token-vs-pixel frontier in prior work.

family_fingerprint.manipulated_variable: compute split (re-encode crops vs generate tokens)

one_line_idea: Best-of-N with a same-model verifier fails for perception because proposer and verifier share percepts: verification gains track proposer-verifier error decorrelation, and cross-encoder verifiers recover most of the oracle gap.
problem: Verifier-guided selection assumes the verifier can score candidates it did not produce, but when verifier and proposer share a vision encoder they plausibly share the misperceptions that caused the bad candidates.
core_hypothesis: Best-of-N gains are a function of proposer-verifier error correlation: same-model verification recovers little of the oracle (pick-the-best) gap on perception tasks, while verifiers with a different vision encoder recover a large share, and measured error correlation predicts the recovery fraction.
falsifiable_prediction: Same-model verifiers recover under 20% of the oracle best-of-N gap on perception-bound tasks; different-encoder verifiers recover at least 40%; recovery fraction correlates with measured error decorrelation at rho of at least 0.5. KILL: the claim dies if same-model verification recovers 40%+ of the oracle gap.
why_important: Best-of-N infrastructure is being built into multimodal serving stacks; knowing that verifier diversity, not verifier strength, is the active ingredient changes what gets deployed.
why_possibly_novel: MODEL SPECULATION (unverified): verifier-guided decoding is studied for text; an error-correlation law governing multimodal verification may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Generate N=16 candidates per question from one open VLM on perception-bound tasks; score with the same VLM, an LLM-only judge on transcripts, and two different-encoder VLM verifiers; compare recovered fractions of the oracle gap against measured pairwise error correlations.
main_risk: Different-encoder verifiers may also differ in language capacity, confounding the encoder-diversity attribution; needs encoder-swapped model pairs where available.
community_default_belief: A model can usefully verify its own outputs because verification is easier than generation.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The verification-is-easier intuition comes from domains with independent checking procedures (code runs, proofs check); shared-percept verification has no independent evidence channel.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One day, single GPU: 200 questions, N=8, same-model vs one different-encoder verifier, recovery fractions. Public data only.

evidence_label.falsifiable_prediction: EXPECTED RESULT (pre-registered threshold; no measured numbers)
evidence_label.prior_work_basis: VERIFIED PRIOR WORK (well-known): best-of-N with verifiers exists for text reasoning; the multimodal error-correlation law is MODEL SPECULATION.

family_fingerprint.manipulated_variable: verifier identity (same model vs different encoder)

one_line_idea: An allocation policy that spends crops and samples per-instance based on a cheap difficulty probe beats uniform allocation at fixed total budget, because the marginal utility of test-time compute varies by an order of magnitude across instances.
problem: Test-time compute is allocated uniformly (same k, same crops for every input), but instance-level marginal utility is plausibly heavy-tailed: most instances need nothing, a few need a lot, and uniform budgets serve neither.
core_hypothesis: A two-signal difficulty probe (draft-answer stability across 2 cheap samples, plus target-size estimate) predicts per-instance marginal utility well enough that adaptive reallocation of a fixed budget strictly dominates uniform spending.
falsifiable_prediction: Adaptive allocation gains at least 3 points over uniform at matched total compute on mixed-difficulty perception benchmarks. KILL: the claim dies if the gain is under 1 point, or if the difficulty probe's utility prediction is uncorrelated (rho under 0.2) with realized per-instance gains.
why_important: Serving costs for multimodal systems scale with worst-case budgets; instance-adaptive allocation converts a fixed budget into strictly more accuracy, which compounds across every deployed query.
why_possibly_novel: MODEL SPECULATION (unverified): adaptive computation is studied inside networks (early exit); loop-level budget reallocation across samples and crops with a utility-prediction validation may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On a mixed benchmark, compute per-instance gain profiles by exhaustive budget sweeps; train/validate the cheap probe against realized utility; then compare adaptive vs uniform policies at three fixed total budgets.
main_risk: Probe cost eats into the budget; the comparison must charge the probe's compute to the adaptive policy honestly.
community_default_belief: Per-query compute policies should be simple and uniform; adaptivity adds complexity without reliable gains.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Uniform budgets are provably wasteful whenever marginal-utility variance is high, and nothing about perception suggests utility is uniform across scenes.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One day, single GPU: 300 instances, exhaustive small sweep to get utility profiles, probe fit, one-budget comparison. Public data only.

evidence_label.falsifiable_prediction: EXPECTED RESULT (pre-registered threshold; no measured numbers)
evidence_label.prior_work_basis: VERIFIED PRIOR WORK (well-known): adaptive computation inside networks exists; loop-level budget reallocation is MODEL SPECULATION.

one_line_idea: Iterative zooming is an anytime algorithm with a predictable profile: the first zoom captures most of the achievable gain on natural-image tasks, and only small-object long-tail tasks keep gaining past two steps.
problem: Zoom-in loops run for fixed depths chosen by intuition; without a gain-profile law, system builders cannot set depth budgets or know which task families justify deep search.
core_hypothesis: Zoom-gain profiles are strongly front-loaded and task-family-dependent in a systematic way: the fraction of total achievable gain captured at step one is high for typical scenes and falls predictably as the ratio of target size to image size shrinks.
falsifiable_prediction: Averaged over natural-image tasks, step-1 zoom captures at least 60% of the total 5-step gain; tasks stratified to the smallest-target decile capture under 40% at step 1. KILL: the claim dies if gains are near-uniform across steps (step-1 share below 35%) on typical scenes.
why_important: A front-loaded law means most deployed zoom loops should have depth 1-2, cutting latency substantially, while identifying precisely the task strata (tiny targets) that justify deeper search.
why_possibly_novel: MODEL SPECULATION (unverified): visual-search agents exist; a quantitative anytime-profile characterization with target-size stratification may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Implement a standard zoom loop over an open VLM; run depths 0-5 on public benchmarks stratified by relative target size; fit gain-vs-step profiles per stratum.
main_risk: Zoom policy quality confounds the profile: a bad policy front-loads nothing; requires both a guided and an oracle-crop upper-bound condition.
community_default_belief: Deeper visual search is better and depth is a quality knob worth scaling.
why_it_might_be_wrong: One zoom fixes resolution mismatch, which is the dominant failure for most scenes; further steps only help when the first crop was wrong, which is the rarer event.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Half a day, single GPU: depths 0-3 on 300 stratified instances, profile fit. Public data only.

evidence_label.community_default_belief: MODEL SPECULATION (inferred from search-depth scaling enthusiasm)
evidence_label.falsifiable_prediction: EXPECTED RESULT (pre-registered threshold; no measured numbers)
evidence_label.prior_work_basis: VERIFIED PRIOR WORK (well-known): iterative visual search loops exist; the anytime-profile law is MODEL SPECULATION.

one_line_idea: A task decomposability score predicts when deep agent loops with a small VLM beat a large VLM at matched FLOPs: loops win only above a decomposability threshold, and the crossover is stable across task families.
problem: Loops-vs-scale is decided by fashion: some teams ship agent pipelines, others ship bigger models, and there is no predictive theory of which architecture wins for a given task at fixed compute.
core_hypothesis: The deciding variable is decomposability — the degree to which a task factors into independently checkable visual subgoals; a score computed from a small pilot (accuracy gain from oracle sub-question decomposition) predicts the loop-vs-scale winner before building either system.
falsifiable_prediction: The decomposability score separates loop-wins from scale-wins with AUC of at least 0.75 across a grid of task families evaluated under iso-FLOP conditions. KILL: the claim dies if AUC is 0.55 or below (no predictive power).
why_important: An ex-ante decision rule for loop-vs-scale saves the field from building the wrong system per task and gives compute-allocation debates an empirical resolution.
why_possibly_novel: MODEL SPECULATION (unverified): loop-vs-scale comparisons exist anecdotally per paper; a predictive decomposability instrument validated across task families may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Assemble 10 public task families; measure decomposability via oracle sub-question pilots; build iso-FLOP loop (small VLM) and scale (large VLM) systems; test whether the score predicts the winner per family.
main_risk: Iso-FLOP normalization across an agent loop and a monolithic model is contestable; requires publishing the accounting and a sensitivity analysis.
community_default_belief: Agent loops and model scale are competing philosophies, and which wins is an empirical accident per benchmark.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Loops pay their overhead back only by reusing intermediate results across subgoals; when a task has no factorization, the loop is a large model with extra steps.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Two days, single GPU: 4 task families, pilot decomposability scores, iso-FLOP comparison with open models at two scales. Public data only.

one_line_idea: Voting over agent-chosen image transformations beats voting over random augmentations at equal vote count: choosing which views to aggregate is itself a perceptual skill the loop can exploit.
problem: Test-time augmentation aggregates predictions over generic transforms chosen blindly, ignoring that the informative view set depends on the specific image and question (glare needs exposure shifts, clutter needs crops, small text needs magnification).
core_hypothesis: An agent that inspects the image and names its suspected failure mode selects transformation sets whose votes are decorrelated where it matters, beating random augmentation voting at matched vote counts — the gain measuring a real introspective-perception capability of the loop.
falsifiable_prediction: Agent-chosen view sets beat random augmentation voting by at least 2 points at k=8 votes on hard perception splits. KILL: the claim dies if the gain is 0.5 points or less, or if a fixed hand-tuned transform set matches the agent's choices (no per-instance skill).
why_important: It would demonstrate a loop-level capability — diagnostic view selection — that no single forward pass possesses, and provide a cheap accuracy lever compatible with any frozen VLM.
why_possibly_novel: MODEL SPECULATION (unverified): test-time augmentation is classical; question-and-image-conditioned transform selection by the loop itself may be untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Implement random-TTA and agent-chosen-TTA at matched k over one open VLM; evaluate on hard perception splits of public benchmarks; ablate with a fixed expert transform set to isolate per-instance selection value.
main_risk: The agent may select transforms that flatter its existing percept (confirmation views), reducing vote diversity instead of increasing it.
community_default_belief: Test-time augmentation is a solved, generic trick; which transforms to use is a dataset-level hyperparameter, not an inference-time decision.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Failure modes are instance-specific, so the optimal view set is too; a loop that can name its likely failure can buy exactly the evidence that discriminates it.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Half a day, single GPU: 300 hard instances, k=8, three conditions (random, fixed-expert, agent-chosen). Public data only.

evidence_label.falsifiable_prediction: EXPECTED RESULT (pre-registered threshold; no measured numbers)
evidence_label.prior_work_basis: VERIFIED PRIOR WORK (well-known): test-time augmentation is classical; agentic per-instance transform selection is MODEL SPECULATION.

one_line_idea: Most of a perception loop's gain can be distilled into a single forward pass by fine-tuning on the loop's own successful traces, implying the loop is primarily a data generator rather than an inference-time necessity.
problem: Agent loops are deployed at inference forever, paying their latency on every query, without asking whether the behavior the loop discovers could be internalized by the base model once.
core_hypothesis: Loop gains on perception tasks come mostly from a re-usable policy (where to look, what to check) rather than from irreducible per-instance search, so LoRA-tuning the base VLM on consistency-filtered loop traces transfers most of the gain into a single pass.
falsifiable_prediction: The distilled single-pass model recovers at least 60% of the loop's accuracy gain at 1x inference cost on held-out data from the same task families. KILL: the claim dies if recovery is under 30% (the loop performs irreducible per-instance computation).
why_important: Whichever way it resolves, the result is decision-grade: either loops are training-data engines and should be amortized, or they perform genuine per-instance search and their latency is the price of the capability.
why_possibly_novel: MODEL SPECULATION (unverified): distilling chain-of-thought is studied for text; a recovery-fraction accounting for perception loops (zoom, verify, re-look) may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run a zoom-and-verify loop over an open VLM to generate 20k traces on public data; filter by cross-run agreement; LoRA-tune the same VLM; compare base, loop, and distilled accuracies on held-out splits.
main_risk: Distillation may overfit the benchmark's task distribution, recovering the gain in-distribution while losing the loop's out-of-distribution flexibility.
community_default_belief: Agent loops add capabilities that inherently require inference-time iteration and cannot live in weights.
why_it_might_be_wrong: If the loop's decisions are largely input-predictable (same zoom for the same kind of scene), they are a function, and functions can be learned.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Two days, single GPU: 5k traces, LoRA tune, three-way comparison on one task family. Public data and open models only.

evidence_label.falsifiable_prediction: EXPECTED RESULT (pre-registered threshold; no measured numbers)
evidence_label.prior_work_basis: VERIFIED PRIOR WORK (well-known): reasoning-trace distillation exists for text; perception-loop recovery accounting is MODEL SPECULATION.

one_line_idea: Perception tasks split into compute-limited and representation-limited families with a measurable signature: cross-sample answer variance under test-time compute predicts whether any loop can help, before running any loop.
problem: Test-time compute sometimes buys perception accuracy and sometimes buys nothing, and the field lacks a cheap diagnostic that says in advance which regime a task instance is in.
core_hypothesis: When the encoder's representation contains the answer but decoding is noisy, samples disagree (high variance) and loops help; when the representation lacks the answer, samples agree on the same error (low variance, wrong mode) and no loop built on the same encoder can help — variance under cheap sampling is therefore a regime detector.
falsifiable_prediction: A variance-based regime classifier predicts the sign of loop gain per task family with at least 70% accuracy. KILL: the claim dies if prediction accuracy is 55% or below (signature uninformative).
why_important: A pre-flight diagnostic for test-time-compute efficacy prevents wasted engineering on representation-limited tasks and routes those to model improvement instead.
why_possibly_novel: MODEL SPECULATION (unverified): variance-based hardness signals exist in active learning; using cross-sample variance as a loop-helpability regime detector for multimodal systems may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: For 10 public task families, measure k=8 answer variance cheaply; independently measure realized gains from a standard zoom-verify loop; test regime prediction on held-out families.
main_risk: Variance conflates decoder temperature artifacts with representational uncertainty; needs a temperature-controlled protocol.
community_default_belief: Whether test-time compute helps is discovered empirically per benchmark after building the loop.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The information needed to predict loop efficacy is already in the base model's sampling behavior; the field just has not read it as a regime signal.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One day, single GPU: 4 task families, variance profiling plus one loop's realized gains. Public data only.

evidence_label.falsifiable_prediction: EXPECTED RESULT (pre-registered threshold; no measured numbers)
evidence_label.prior_work_basis: MODEL SPECULATION: variance signals exist in active learning; regime-detection use for loops not verified.

family_fingerprint.measurement_family: regime-prediction accuracy for loop gain sign

one_line_idea: Self-correction in vision agents fixes reasoning slips but not perception errors: revision rates conditioned on error type are strongly asymmetric because the loop re-reads its own percept instead of re-perceiving.
problem: Self-correction prompts are applied uniformly to multimodal outputs, but the mechanism of revision — re-reading the transcript — can only fix errors that are visible in the transcript, which perception errors are not.
core_hypothesis: Revision operates on the verbal trace, not on the image: errors introduced during reasoning are detectable and correctable from text alone, while errors introduced at perception are invisible to the loop, producing a large, stable revision-rate asymmetry by error type.
falsifiable_prediction: The revision rate for perception-typed errors is below 0.33x the rate for reasoning-typed errors under identical self-correction prompts. KILL: the claim dies if the ratio exceeds 0.67 (no meaningful asymmetry).
