why_important: The asymmetry explains why self-correction results look inconsistent across benchmarks (they differ in error-type mix) and dictates that perception errors need re-perception mechanisms, not better critique prompts.
why_possibly_novel: MODEL SPECULATION (unverified): self-correction limits are debated for text models; an error-type-conditioned revision accounting for vision agents may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Collect first-pass errors on public multimodal benchmarks; type them (perception vs reasoning) via rubric; apply standard self-correction; measure per-type revision and repair rates.
main_risk: Error typing is judgment-laden; requires dual independent tagging and agreement reporting.
community_default_belief: Self-correction is a general capability that improves outputs regardless of where the error came from.
why_it_might_be_wrong: A loop that never re-encodes pixels has no channel through which a wrong percept could be noticed, let alone fixed.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One day, single GPU: 300 errors typed, one revision round, per-type repair rates. Public data only.

evidence_label.falsifiable_prediction: EXPECTED RESULT (pre-registered threshold; no measured numbers)
evidence_label.prior_work_basis: VERIFIED PRIOR WORK (well-known): self-correction debates exist for LLMs; error-type-conditioned accounting in vision loops is MODEL SPECULATION.

one_line_idea: Below a measurable critic-precision threshold, verify-then-revise loops are net negative: flips from correct to wrong outnumber repairs, and the break-even precision can be estimated in advance from the flip matrix.
problem: Verification loops are added to pipelines on the assumption that more checking cannot hurt, but every false objection risks flipping a correct answer, and no deployment guidance says how good the critic must be to pay for itself.
core_hypothesis: Revision behavior is governed by a simple accounting identity over the flip matrix (repair rate times error mass vs corruption rate times correct mass); the break-even critic precision derived from a small pilot predicts whether any given critic will help or hurt at scale.
falsifiable_prediction: Break-even precision estimated from a 100-instance pilot predicts the realized sign of the revision effect on a 10x larger evaluation within a precision margin of 0.1. KILL: the claim dies if pilot-estimated break-even misses the realized threshold by more than 0.2 (flip matrix unstable).
why_important: It converts add-a-verifier from a faith-based decision into a measured one, and explains published contradictions where verification helps one system and hurts another.
why_possibly_novel: MODEL SPECULATION (unverified): net-negative self-correction has been observed for text models; a predictive break-even calculus for vision-agent critics may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: For three critic variants of different strictness over one open VLM pipeline, estimate flip matrices on pilots, derive break-even points, then verify predicted signs on large held-out splits.
main_risk: Flip matrices may drift with content domain, so the pilot must be drawn from the deployment distribution.
community_default_belief: A verification pass is a safe addition: at worst it does nothing, at best it catches errors.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Agents are suggestible; a wrong objection from a trusted-looking critic flips correct answers, and the loss side of the ledger is invisible unless measured.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Half a day, single GPU: one critic, 100-instance pilot flip matrix, sign prediction test on 500 instances. Public data only.

evidence_label.falsifiable_prediction: EXPECTED RESULT (pre-registered threshold; no measured numbers)
evidence_label.prior_work_basis: VERIFIED PRIOR WORK (well-known): net-negative self-correction reports exist for LLMs; the predictive break-even calculus is MODEL SPECULATION.

one_line_idea: Requiring critics to cite pixel evidence — a crop or mark accompanying every objection — turns marginal verification loops into positive ones, because ungrounded objections drive most wrong flips.
problem: Free-text critics object fluently whether or not they saw anything wrong, and the reviser cannot distinguish grounded objections from confabulated ones, so corrupting flips ride in with repairs.
core_hypothesis: The damage in verification loops is concentrated in evidence-free objections; imposing an evidence-citation contract (every objection must attach the region it is about) suppresses confabulated critiques more than it suppresses true ones, moving the loop's flip matrix to net positive.
falsifiable_prediction: Evidence-pointing critics improve net revision gain by at least 3 points over free-text critics at equal compute, and the fraction of wrong flips drops by at least 40% relative. KILL: the claim dies if the net-gain improvement is 1 point or less.
why_important: A contract-level fix that makes verification safe-by-default would unblock verifier deployment across multimodal pipelines that currently skip it after bad experiences.
why_possibly_novel: MODEL SPECULATION (unverified): grounded critique formats appear in specific systems; the causal claim that evidence contracts flip the sign of revision loops may be untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run matched revision loops (free-text vs evidence-contract critics) over one open VLM on public benchmarks; log flip matrices; compare net gains and the composition of suppressed objections.
main_risk: Forcing evidence may suppress valid global objections (lighting, style, count-across-image) that have no single region to cite.
community_default_belief: Critic quality is about the critic model's strength; format contracts are cosmetic.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Requiring evidence changes the critic's decision problem from 'write a plausible critique' to 'find a failure', and only the second correlates with truth.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One day, single GPU: 300 instances, two critic contracts, flip-matrix comparison. Public data only.

evidence_label.falsifiable_prediction: EXPECTED RESULT (pre-registered threshold; no measured numbers)
evidence_label.prior_work_basis: MODEL SPECULATION: grounded-critique formats exist in scattered systems; the sign-flip causal claim is unverified.

one_line_idea: Structured visual outputs should be verified visually: rendering predicted boxes or layouts back onto the image and asking a fresh model 'is this consistent' catches error classes that text-based verification of the same predictions never flags.
problem: Pipelines verify structured outputs (boxes, layouts, reading order) by reasoning over their textual serialization, where geometric absurdities — overlapping labels, boxes off the object, impossible sizes — are invisible.
core_hypothesis: Re-rendering closes the loop through perception: a verifier that sees the prediction drawn on the image detects geometric and relational errors that are undetectable from coordinates-as-text, adding a complementary error channel rather than a redundant one.
falsifiable_prediction: Render-back verification catches at least 25% of the errors missed by text verification at equal verifier compute, with the two methods' caught-error sets overlapping less than 60%. KILL: the claim dies if render-back adds under 8% coverage of missed errors.
why_important: It establishes a general principle — verify in the modality where the error lives — that applies to any pipeline emitting spatial structure, from document parsing to robotic scene graphs.
why_possibly_novel: MODEL SPECULATION (unverified): visualization for human debugging is standard; render-back as an automated in-loop verification channel with error-set accounting may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Take an open pipeline producing boxes/layouts on public images; inject and collect natural errors; run text-serialization verification vs render-back verification with the same verifier model; compare caught-error sets.
main_risk: Rendering style (color, thickness, label placement) may itself bias the verifier; requires style ablations.
community_default_belief: Verification is a reasoning activity over the pipeline's outputs; serialized coordinates contain everything the verifier needs.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Geometric wrongness is a perceptual gestalt, cheap to see and expensive to compute from numbers; text verification asks the model to do the expensive version.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Half a day, single GPU: 200 predictions with known errors, both verification channels, caught-set comparison. Public data only.

evidence_label.falsifiable_prediction: EXPECTED RESULT (pre-registered threshold; no measured numbers)
evidence_label.prior_work_basis: MODEL SPECULATION: render-for-humans is standard practice; automated render-back verification accounting is unverified.

one_line_idea: Self-verification loops have attractors: iterating verify-revise converges within a few steps to answers that are stable but wrong on a measurable fraction of instances, and convergence speed does not predict correctness.
problem: Practitioners run revision until the answer stops changing and read stability as a correctness signal, but nothing guarantees the loop's fixed points coincide with truth.
core_hypothesis: Verify-revise dynamics form a map with multiple attractors determined by the model's priors and the transcript, not by the image; a non-trivial fraction of instances converge to stable wrong answers from any reasonable start, and convergence speed is uninformative about which attractor was reached.
falsifiable_prediction: At least 15% of converged answers are stable-but-wrong, and the correlation between convergence step count and correctness is negligible (absolute rho under 0.2). KILL: the claim dies if stable-wrong is under 5% or convergence speed strongly predicts correctness (rho above 0.5).
why_important: It invalidates stability as a stopping-time correctness proxy — a practice embedded in many agent implementations — and motivates restart-diversity or cross-encoder escape mechanisms.
why_possibly_novel: MODEL SPECULATION (unverified): fixed-point framing of revision dynamics with attractor accounting for vision agents may be new; text-model self-correction studies do not usually iterate to convergence.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Iterate verify-revise to convergence (cap 8 rounds) from three different initializations per instance on public benchmarks; classify converged answers by correctness; test whether initialization changes the attractor and whether speed predicts truth.
main_risk: Convergence definitions (exact string vs semantic equivalence) change the numbers; both must be reported.
community_default_belief: If repeated self-checks stop finding problems, the answer is probably right.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The loop re-samples from the same conditional distribution each round; a confident wrong mode is exactly as absorbing as a correct one.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One day, single GPU: 200 instances, convergence runs from 2 starts, attractor statistics. Public data only.

evidence_label.falsifiable_prediction: EXPECTED RESULT (pre-registered threshold; no measured numbers)
evidence_label.prior_work_basis: MODEL SPECULATION: no verified attractor accounting for multimodal revision loops.

one_line_idea: Verifying visual claims via entailed consequence questions ('if X, then Y should be visible — check Y') outperforms direct re-asking, because consequence checks decorrelate the verifier's percept from the proposer's.
problem: Direct verification re-asks the same question and predictably re-samples the same percept; the loop needs verification queries whose answers are informative about the claim but perceptually independent of the original judgment.
core_hypothesis: Claims about images entail secondary observables (shadows, occlusion patterns, co-occurring parts, geometric consequences); querying those observables engages different visual evidence than the original question, so consequence-based verification detects false claims that direct re-asking confirms.
falsifiable_prediction: Consequence-question verification improves false-claim detection by at least 10 points over direct re-asking at equal verifier compute. KILL: the claim dies if the improvement is 3 points or less.
why_important: It provides a principled recipe for building verification queries — derive entailments, check the cheapest decorrelated one — replacing the useless default of asking again louder.
why_possibly_novel: MODEL SPECULATION (unverified): entailment-based checking exists for text claims; visual-consequence derivation as a verification mechanism in agent loops may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build a claim set with ground truth over public images; have the loop derive 2 consequence questions per claim; compare detection rates of direct re-ask vs consequence checking with the same verifier model.
main_risk: Consequence derivation itself can be wrong (false entailments), converting verification errors into derivation errors; the pipeline must score derivation validity separately.
community_default_belief: Verification means checking the answer — re-asking with a critical prompt is the natural implementation.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Repeated queries into the same encoder are correlated draws; only changing what is asked changes what is looked at.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One day, single GPU: 200 claims (half false by construction), both verification modes, detection comparison. Public data only.

evidence_label.community_default_belief: MODEL SPECULATION (inferred from re-ask verification defaults)
evidence_label.falsifiable_prediction: EXPECTED RESULT (pre-registered threshold; no measured numbers)
evidence_label.prior_work_basis: MODEL SPECULATION: textual entailment checking exists; visual-consequence verification unverified.

family_fingerprint.manipulated_variable: query type (direct re-ask vs derived consequence)

one_line_idea: Revision gains decay geometrically across rounds with a stable ratio: one revision captures most of the achievable repair, making multi-round self-correction schedules mostly wasted compute.
problem: Revision-round counts are chosen arbitrarily (3 is common) with no empirical law describing marginal returns, so schedulers cannot justify budgets.
core_hypothesis: The population of repairable errors is exhausted front-first: errors fixable by the loop's mechanism get fixed in round one, and later rounds churn on unfixable (perception-borne) errors, producing a geometric decay in marginal gain with a ratio stable across tasks and models.
falsifiable_prediction: Combined gain from rounds 2 and onward is under 50% of round-1 gain across tasks and two open models. KILL: the claim dies if round-2 gain matches or exceeds round-1 gain in most settings.
why_important: A stable decay law gives an immediate scheduling rule (one round unless task-specific evidence says otherwise) and frees compute for mechanisms that attack the unfixable remainder.
why_possibly_novel: MODEL SPECULATION (unverified): multi-round revision curves are rarely reported; a cross-task decay-ratio characterization for vision agents may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run 4 revision rounds on three public multimodal benchmarks with two open models; log per-round net gains; fit decay ratios and test cross-setting stability.
main_risk: Gains per round are small, so distinguishing geometric decay from noise requires large samples; power analysis first.
community_default_belief: More revision rounds monotonically improve quality, budget permitting.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Round one already saw every error the transcript exposes; without new evidence entering the loop, later rounds re-litigate the same information.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One day, single GPU: 500 instances, 3 rounds, per-round gain curve. Public data only.

evidence_label.community_default_belief: MODEL SPECULATION (inferred from multi-round scheduling practice)
evidence_label.falsifiable_prediction: EXPECTED RESULT (pre-registered threshold; no measured numbers)
evidence_label.prior_work_basis: MODEL SPECULATION: no verified cross-task decay-ratio law in prior work.

one_line_idea: A small library of specialized critics keyed to a fixed visual-error taxonomy (mislocalization, miscount, attribute swap, relation flip, hallucinated object) beats one general critic at equal cost, because critic instructions act as error priors.
problem: General-purpose critics must simultaneously hypothesize what kind of error occurred and whether it occurred, diluting attention across error types; the loop never tells the critic what to look for.
core_hypothesis: Critique is a detection problem with a prior: routing each output to type-specialized critics (or running a cheap type classifier first) concentrates the verifier's capacity on the likely failure, raising detection at fixed compute relative to one broad critic.
falsifiable_prediction: Taxonomy-routed critics beat a general critic by at least 3 points net revision gain at equal total compute. KILL: the claim dies if the advantage is 1 point or less, or if random routing matches taxonomy routing (specialization content irrelevant).
why_important: It reframes critic design from prompt-crafting art to portfolio engineering over an error taxonomy — modular, measurable, and transferable across pipelines.
why_possibly_novel: MODEL SPECULATION (unverified): specialized judges exist in some eval settings; a routed critic portfolio with equal-compute accounting inside revision loops may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Define the 5-type taxonomy; build per-type critic prompts and a lightweight router; compare against a strong general critic at matched compute on public benchmarks with typed error ground truth.
main_risk: Router errors could send outputs to the wrong specialist, and taxonomy coverage gaps would leave novel error types undetected.
community_default_belief: One strong critic model with a good general prompt is the right architecture; specialization is unnecessary overhead.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Detection with an informative prior beats detection without one at fixed capacity — a basic signal-detection argument the loop currently ignores.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One day, single GPU: 300 typed-error instances, routed vs general critics, net-gain comparison. Public data only.

evidence_label.falsifiable_prediction: EXPECTED RESULT (pre-registered threshold; no measured numbers)
evidence_label.prior_work_basis: MODEL SPECULATION: specialized judges appear in eval contexts; routed critic portfolios in revision loops unverified.

family_fingerprint.measurement_family: net revision gain at matched compute

one_line_idea: Verifiers inherit proposer percepts through the transcript: verifiers shown only the image and the bare answer catch more perception errors than verifiers shown the full chain-of-thought, reversing the assumed value of context.
problem: Verification prompts include the proposer's full reasoning on the theory that more context helps the verifier, but the reasoning is also a channel through which the proposer's misperception colonizes the verifier's judgment.
core_hypothesis: Transcript exposure induces percept inheritance: a verifier that reads the proposer's description of the image tends to see the image that way, so blinding the verifier to everything except image and answer forces an independent look and raises perception-error detection.
falsifiable_prediction: Blinded verifiers detect at least 15% more perception-typed errors than full-context verifiers at equal compute, while reasoning-typed error detection may favor full context. KILL: the claim dies if full-context verifiers win on perception errors too.
why_important: Verifier-context design is a free parameter in every pipeline; if blinding helps where it matters most (perception), current defaults are backwards for multimodal verification.
why_possibly_novel: MODEL SPECULATION (unverified): anchoring effects are known in human review; a controlled context-exposure study for multimodal verifiers with error-type stratification may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On typed-error sets over public images, run verifiers under three exposure levels (image+answer, +final rationale, +full chain); measure detection by error type at matched compute.
main_risk: Blinded verifiers lack task context and may over-flag valid answers, so precision must be tracked alongside detection.
community_default_belief: Give the verifier everything the proposer produced; context can only inform its judgment.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Reading a persuasive but wrong description before looking is textbook anchoring; models trained on human text plausibly inherit the bias.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Half a day, single GPU: 200 typed errors, two exposure levels, per-type detection rates. Public data only.

evidence_label.falsifiable_prediction: EXPECTED RESULT (pre-registered threshold; no measured numbers)
evidence_label.prior_work_basis: MODEL SPECULATION: human anchoring literature exists; multimodal verifier-exposure study unverified.

one_line_idea: Step-level verification of intermediate tool outputs beats final-answer verification for multi-step visual tasks at matched verification budget, and the advantage grows with chain length.
problem: Verification budgets are spent on final answers, where errors from early steps have already been laundered into fluent conclusions that are hard to falsify without re-doing the whole task.
core_hypothesis: Errors are cheapest to catch where they enter: intermediate tool outputs are small, concrete, and checkable against the image, so allocating the same verification compute across steps instead of the final answer yields higher end-task accuracy, with the advantage scaling in chain depth.
falsifiable_prediction: Process-level verification beats outcome-level verification by at least 4 points on tasks with 3+ steps at matched budget, and the gap increases with chain length. KILL: the claim dies if the gap is 1 point or less at depth 3+, or shrinks with depth.
why_important: It transfers the process-supervision lesson from math reasoning into vision pipelines with an operational budget-allocation rule that any framework can adopt today.
why_possibly_novel: MODEL SPECULATION (unverified): process supervision is established for mathematical reasoning; matched-budget process-vs-outcome verification accounting for visual tool chains may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Instrument an open multi-step pipeline on public compositional tasks; implement both verification allocations at equal compute; compare end-task accuracy stratified by chain depth.
main_risk: Step verifiers need per-tool rubrics whose quality varies, confounding the allocation comparison with rubric quality.
community_default_belief: Checking the final answer is the efficient way to verify; intermediate steps are means, not claims worth budget.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Early errors compound and camouflage; the final answer is the most expensive place to detect what a step-level check would have caught for pennies.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One day, single GPU: 200 multi-step tasks, both allocations at one budget, depth-stratified comparison. Public data only.

evidence_label.falsifiable_prediction: EXPECTED RESULT (pre-registered threshold; no measured numbers)
evidence_label.prior_work_basis: VERIFIED PRIOR WORK (well-known): process supervision for math reasoning exists; the matched-budget visual-chain claim is MODEL SPECULATION.

one_line_idea: Visual programs beat end-to-end VLM answering only above a measurable compositional-depth threshold: below it the program machinery is pure overhead, and the crossover depth is stable across program frameworks.
problem: Visual programming systems report aggregate wins or losses against end-to-end VLMs, but aggregates hide the variable that plausibly decides every instance: how many composition steps the query actually requires.
core_hypothesis: Program decomposition pays a fixed overhead (synthesis errors, interface losses) and buys a per-step advantage (isolated, checkable subproblems); the balance tips at a characteristic compositional depth, and that crossover is a stable property of the paradigm rather than of one framework.
falsifiable_prediction: Stratifying queries by annotated compositional depth shows programs losing at depth 1, with a crossover at depth 2-3 that shifts by less than one depth unit across two open program frameworks. KILL: the claim dies if programs win at depth 1 or never cross over by depth 4.
why_important: A depth-based routing rule (send shallow queries to the VLM, deep ones to programs) would beat both pure paradigms and settle when the program abstraction is worth its cost.
why_possibly_novel: MODEL SPECULATION (unverified): visual programming frameworks report benchmark aggregates; a depth-stratified crossover law with cross-framework stability may be unmeasured.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Annotate compositional depth for public compositional-VQA queries; run an open visual-programming framework and a matched end-to-end VLM; plot accuracy-vs-depth for both and locate crossovers across two frameworks.
main_risk: Depth annotation is contestable; needs two independent annotation schemes (syntactic operator count and human judgment) shown to agree.
community_default_belief: Visual programming either is or is not better than end-to-end answering — the comparison is framework-level, decided by aggregate benchmark scores.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Both paradigms hide a depth-dependent tradeoff that aggregates average away; the interesting object is the crossover, not the mean.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One day, single GPU: 300 depth-annotated queries, one open framework vs one open VLM, accuracy-vs-depth curves. Public data only.

evidence_label.falsifiable_prediction: EXPECTED RESULT (pre-registered threshold; no measured numbers)
evidence_label.prior_work_basis: VERIFIED PRIOR WORK (well-known): visual programming frameworks such as VisProg and ViperGPT exist; the depth-crossover law is MODEL SPECULATION.

one_line_idea: Most visual-program failures collapse into a short list of primitive-misuse patterns, so a fixed library of about ten automatic repair rules recovers a large share of failed executions without improving the planner.
problem: Visual-program failures are treated as planner weaknesses requiring better LLMs, but the failure mass may sit in a small, enumerable set of mechanical misuse patterns (wrong argument order, missing existence check, scalar-where-set-expected) that rules can fix.
core_hypothesis: The failure distribution over program executions is heavy-headed: a compact rule library targeting the top misuse patterns (detected from execution traces, applied as automatic rewrites) recovers a substantial fraction of failures at negligible cost, bounding how much planner intelligence is actually missing.
falsifiable_prediction: The top-10 repair rules recover at least 30% of failed executions on held-out queries. KILL: the claim dies if recovery is under 10% (failures are diffuse and planner-bound after all).
why_important: If a static rule pass recovers a third of failures, the field is over-attributing program errors to planning intelligence and under-investing in execution-layer engineering.
why_possibly_novel: MODEL SPECULATION (unverified): program repair is a mature field for conventional code; a misuse-pattern census plus repair-rule recovery accounting for visual programs may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Collect 1,000 failed executions from an open visual-programming framework on public queries; cluster failure signatures; write rules for the top patterns; measure recovery on a held-out failure set.
main_risk: Rules that fix executions may still yield wrong answers (execution success is not correctness); both metrics must be reported.
community_default_belief: Visual-program quality tracks planner LLM quality; fixing failures means upgrading or fine-tuning the planner.
why_it_might_be_wrong: LLM planners make systematic, not random, API mistakes — and systematic mistakes are exactly what static rules catch.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One day, single GPU: 300 failures clustered, 5 rules written, recovery measured on 200 held-out failures. Public data only.

evidence_label.falsifiable_prediction: EXPECTED RESULT (pre-registered threshold; no measured numbers)
evidence_label.prior_work_basis: VERIFIED PRIOR WORK (well-known): automated program repair exists for conventional code; visual-program repair-rule accounting is MODEL SPECULATION.

one_line_idea: Program abstractions assume deterministic subroutines, but resampling stochastic primitives flips visual-program answers at a rate that rivals planner-quality differences, making single-run program evaluations unstable as system claims.
problem: Visual programs compose primitives that are themselves stochastic model calls, violating the determinism assumption that makes program semantics meaningful; the size of this violation is unmeasured.
core_hypothesis: Answer identity under primitive resampling is fragile in proportion to program depth and to how many primitives sit on the answer's critical path; the induced answer-flip rate is large enough to rival gaps attributed to planner choice, so program behavior is a distribution, not a value.
falsifiable_prediction: Resampling primitives (fixed program, fixed image) flips at least 10% of answers on multi-step queries, and flip rate grows with critical-path length. KILL: the claim dies if the flip rate is under 3% (determinism approximately holds).
why_important: It changes both evaluation practice (report answer distributions for programs) and design practice (add determinization layers — argmax settings, consensus wrappers — at primitive boundaries).
why_possibly_novel: MODEL SPECULATION (unverified): nondeterminism of model calls is known; quantifying its violation of program semantics in visual programs, with critical-path scaling, may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Fix programs and images from an open framework; resample primitives 10 times per instance; measure answer-flip rates by program depth and critical-path composition; compare to planner-swap disagreement.
main_risk: Some primitives are deterministic at temperature zero; the study must characterize which primitive classes carry the stochasticity.
community_default_belief: A synthesized program is an interpretable, reproducible artifact — the point of the paradigm is that execution is legible and stable.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Transparency of structure is not stability of behavior when every node is a sampled model call.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Half a day, single GPU: 200 programs, 5 resamples each, flip-rate by depth. Public data only.

evidence_label.community_default_belief: MODEL SPECULATION (inferred from interpretability claims for programs)
evidence_label.falsifiable_prediction: EXPECTED RESULT (pre-registered threshold; no measured numbers)
evidence_label.prior_work_basis: MODEL SPECULATION: model-call nondeterminism is known; program-semantics violation accounting unverified.

one_line_idea: Visual programs are less faithful than they look: when a primitive fails silently, controllers often emit answers from language priors while presenting them as program outputs, and counterfactual step-perturbation quantifies how often execution is bypassed.
problem: The credibility of visual programs rests on answers being computed by the displayed program, but the LLM that assembles the final response can fall back on its priors when execution returns nothing useful — with no visible trace of the substitution.
core_hypothesis: Execution bypass is common and measurable: counterfactually flipping a decisive intermediate output should flip the answer under faithful execution, so the rate of unchanged answers under decisive flips directly measures how often the program is theater.
falsifiable_prediction: At least 20% of answers remain unchanged when a decisive intermediate output is counterfactually flipped. KILL: the claim dies if under 5% of answers survive decisive flips (execution is faithful).
why_important: Program-based systems are marketed as auditable; a quantified bypass rate either validates that claim or exposes it, and the counterfactual-flip harness becomes a standard faithfulness meter.
why_possibly_novel: MODEL SPECULATION (unverified): faithfulness of chain-of-thought is studied for text; counterfactual execution-perturbation as a faithfulness meter for visual programs may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Instrument an open framework to intercept and flip decisive intermediate values (existence bits, counts, comparisons) on public queries; measure answer-invariance rates and stratify by whether the original execution had failed silently.
main_risk: Deciding which intermediate is decisive requires care; a non-decisive flip legitimately leaves answers unchanged and would inflate the bypass estimate.
community_default_belief: The program you see is the computation you get; visual programming trades accuracy for transparency honestly.
why_it_might_be_wrong: The final-response step is still a language model conditioned on a question it can often answer from priors; nothing in the loop forces it to defer to execution.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One day, single GPU: 200 queries, decisive-flip harness on one framework, invariance rate. Public data only.

evidence_label.falsifiable_prediction: EXPECTED RESULT (pre-registered threshold; no measured numbers)
evidence_label.prior_work_basis: VERIFIED PRIOR WORK (well-known): CoT-faithfulness studies exist for text models; the visual-program bypass meter is MODEL SPECULATION.

one_line_idea: Real query streams concentrate on few program skeletons, so caching and re-instantiating the top skeletons amortizes synthesis: coverage-vs-cache-size follows a heavy-tailed law exploitable for systems.
problem: Every query triggers fresh program synthesis — the most expensive and error-prone stage — even though most queries are structural repeats (count the X, compare attribute of A and B, find the X left of Y) differing only in slot values.
core_hypothesis: Abstracting synthesized programs into slotted skeletons reveals a heavy-tailed reuse distribution; retrieving and re-instantiating cached skeletons for matching queries cuts synthesis errors and latency while covering most traffic with a small cache.
falsifiable_prediction: The top-20 skeletons cover at least 60% of a public compositional-VQA query set, and cached instantiation matches fresh synthesis accuracy within 1 point at a fraction of the synthesis cost. KILL: the claim dies if top-20 coverage is under 35% (reuse too diffuse to exploit).
why_important: Amortized synthesis changes visual programming's cost profile from per-query LLM calls to cheap retrieval plus slot filling, making the paradigm deployable at scale.
why_possibly_novel: MODEL SPECULATION (unverified): query-plan caching is standard in databases; a skeleton-reuse census and cache architecture for visual programs may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Synthesize programs for 5,000 public queries; canonicalize into skeletons; measure the coverage curve; build retrieval-plus-instantiation and compare accuracy and cost against fresh synthesis on held-out queries.
main_risk: Skeleton matching errors substitute wrong programs silently; the matcher needs a confidence gate with fallback to fresh synthesis.
community_default_belief: Program synthesis is inherently per-query; the planner must reason about each question individually.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Natural question distributions are templatic; the planner keeps re-deriving the same dozen plans and charging full price each time.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Half a day, single GPU: synthesize for 1,000 queries, canonicalize, plot the coverage curve. Public data only.

evidence_label.community_default_belief: MODEL SPECULATION (inferred from per-query synthesis practice)
evidence_label.falsifiable_prediction: EXPECTED RESULT (pre-registered threshold; no measured numbers)
evidence_label.prior_work_basis: VERIFIED PRIOR WORK (well-known): plan caching exists in databases; visual-program skeleton caching is MODEL SPECULATION.

one_line_idea: Adding a lightweight type system over visual-program primitives (region, entity-set, scalar, boolean) prevents a major share of wrong answers, because type confusion at step boundaries — not planning — is the dominant failure.
problem: Visual-program primitives exchange untyped values: a region where an entity-set was expected, a count where a boolean was expected — and executions proceed silently to wrong answers instead of failing at the boundary.
core_hypothesis: A four-type discipline with checked coercions at step boundaries converts silent wrong answers into either correct coercions or loud failures that trigger resynthesis; the wrong-answer reduction it achieves measures how much of the paradigm's error mass is boundary confusion rather than bad plans.
falsifiable_prediction: Type checking plus standard coercion rules cuts wrong answers by at least 15% relative on compositional public benchmarks. KILL: the claim dies if the reduction is under 5% (boundary confusion is marginal).
why_important: It imports the cheapest, oldest lesson of programming languages into a paradigm currently written as untyped glue — and quantifies the payoff, including for LLM-orchestrated pipelines that end in promptable segmentation primitives.
why_possibly_novel: MODEL SPECULATION (unverified): typed DSLs are ancient in PL research; a measured wrong-answer accounting attributable to type discipline in visual programs may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Retrofit type annotations onto an open framework's primitives; implement boundary checks and coercions; A/B fixed queries with and without the discipline; attribute changed outcomes to boundary events in the traces.
main_risk: Coercion rules could themselves introduce errors (silently coercing an entity-set to its count where the plan wanted existence).
community_default_belief: Visual-program errors come from planning and primitive quality; the glue code between steps is trivial.
why_it_might_be_wrong: LLM planners emit plausible-looking argument wiring with systematic type slips, and untyped execution lets every slip through to the answer.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One day, single GPU: type-annotate 10 primitives, run 300 queries A/B, boundary-event attribution. Public data only.

evidence_label.community_default_belief: MODEL SPECULATION (inferred from untyped framework designs)
evidence_label.falsifiable_prediction: EXPECTED RESULT (pre-registered threshold; no measured numbers)
evidence_label.prior_work_basis: VERIFIED PRIOR WORK (well-known): typed DSL benefits are established in PL; the visual-program accounting is MODEL SPECULATION.

one_line_idea: Planners told each primitive's empirical error profile write different and better programs — inserting redundancy and cross-checks where primitives are weak — showing program synthesis should condition on tool reliability, not just tool signatures.
problem: Planners see primitive signatures (name, arguments, return type) but not reliability, so they compose a fragile counting primitive and a robust existence primitive with equal trust, producing plans that are optimal only in a world of perfect tools.
core_hypothesis: Injecting measured per-primitive error profiles into the synthesis prompt changes plan structure in predictable directions (redundant paths around weak primitives, cheap existence checks before expensive chains, preference for reliable primitives at critical nodes) and those structural changes improve end-task accuracy.
falsifiable_prediction: Reliability-aware synthesis beats signature-only synthesis by at least 3 points end-task, and generated plans show a measurable structural shift (higher redundancy around low-reliability primitives). KILL: the claim dies if the gain is 1 point or less or plan structure does not change.
why_important: It establishes reliability as a first-class input to program synthesis over imperfect learned components — a design principle for every orchestrated pipeline, including segmentation-tool chains.
why_possibly_novel: MODEL SPECULATION (unverified): fault-tolerant planning is classical in robotics; reliability-conditioned LLM program synthesis over vision primitives with structural-shift accounting may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Measure error profiles for 8 primitives on pilot data; run matched synthesis with and without profiles in the prompt on public compositional queries; compare accuracy and plan-structure statistics.
main_risk: The planner may ignore the profiles (the metadata-consumption problem) or over-hedge every plan into expensive redundancy.
community_default_belief: Better plans come from better planners; tool APIs are the fixed vocabulary the planner works with.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Optimal composition under component noise differs from noiseless composition, and the planner can only account for noise it is told about.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One day, single GPU: profiles for 5 primitives, 300 queries A/B, accuracy plus redundancy statistics. Public data only.

evidence_label.community_default_belief: MODEL SPECULATION (inferred from signature-only prompting practice)
evidence_label.falsifiable_prediction: EXPECTED RESULT (pre-registered threshold; no measured numbers)
evidence_label.prior_work_basis: VERIFIED PRIOR WORK (well-known): fault-tolerant planning exists in robotics; reliability-conditioned visual-program synthesis is MODEL SPECULATION.

one_line_idea: Disagreement among multiple valid programs synthesized for the same query detects question ambiguity, not model failure: program-set disagreement predicts human answer disagreement and triggers useful clarification requests.
problem: When differently-structured programs for one query return different answers, systems treat it as noise to vote away; but structurally distinct valid programs formalize different readings of the question, so their disagreement may carry information about the question itself.
core_hypothesis: Program-set disagreement is an ambiguity meter: queries where diverse valid programs disagree are disproportionately those where humans also disagree, and surfacing the programs' divergent readings yields clarification questions users accept as legitimate.
falsifiable_prediction: Program-disagreement flags correlate with human answer disagreement at rho of at least 0.4, beating an answer-resampling baseline at matched compute. KILL: the claim dies if rho is under 0.15 or resampling matches program diversity.
why_important: Ambiguity detection is a missing capability in deployed VQA; deriving it from the program abstraction gives the paradigm a unique payoff beyond accuracy — knowing when the question, not the model, is the problem.
why_possibly_novel: MODEL SPECULATION (unverified): ambiguity detection via output sampling exists; using structural program diversity as the ambiguity signal, validated against human disagreement, may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Synthesize 5 diverse programs per query on public datasets that include multiple human answers; correlate program-disagreement with human-disagreement; compare against resampling baselines at matched compute.
main_risk: Program diversity is hard to enforce; near-duplicate programs would make the signal degenerate to resampling.
community_default_belief: Disagreement between runs is model noise; the fix is voting, and the question is assumed well-posed.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Distinct valid programs are distinct formalizations; when formalizations diverge, the informal question was ambiguous — a property voting actively hides.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One day, single GPU: 300 queries with multi-annotator answers, 3 programs each, correlation test. Public data only.

evidence_label.falsifiable_prediction: EXPECTED RESULT (pre-registered threshold; no measured numbers)
evidence_label.prior_work_basis: MODEL SPECULATION: sampling-based ambiguity signals exist; program-structural ambiguity detection unverified.

one_line_idea: Visual programs are their own data engines: executing synthesized programs on procedurally generated scenes yields verified supervision that fine-tunes the planner, improving synthesis on real queries without human labels.
problem: Planner fine-tuning needs (query, correct program) pairs that do not exist at scale; but on procedurally generated scenes the ground truth of every executable claim is known, so program correctness is checkable for free.
core_hypothesis: A closed self-improvement loop — synthesize programs, execute on procedural scenes with known state, keep programs whose outputs match scene ground truth, fine-tune the planner on the survivors — transfers to real-image queries because program structure, not scene texture, is what the planner learns.
falsifiable_prediction: Program-curriculum tuning improves planner execution-success and answer accuracy by at least 5 points on held-out real-image compositional queries. KILL: the claim dies if real-query improvement is 1 point or less (structure does not transfer) or if performance degrades on non-compositional tasks by more than 2 points.
why_important: It gives visual programming a self-improvement mechanism with verified rewards — the property that made program synthesis for code take off — without any annotation budget.
why_possibly_novel: MODEL SPECULATION (unverified): self-training with execution feedback is established for code generation; the procedural-scene verified-reward loop for visual-program planners may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Build a procedural scene generator with queryable ground truth; run the loop for one round (10k synthesized programs, filter, LoRA-tune an open planner); evaluate on held-out real-image compositional benchmarks.
main_risk: Procedural scenes may teach programs that exploit generator regularities (fixed vocabularies, clean segmentations) that break on real images.
community_default_belief: Planner improvement requires human-written programs or distillation from a stronger LLM.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Verified execution feedback is a stronger training signal than imitation, and vision uniquely allows manufacturing worlds where verification is exact.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Two days, single GPU: small procedural generator, 2k filtered programs, LoRA tune, held-out real-query delta. Public/procedural data only.

evidence_label.community_default_belief: MODEL SPECULATION (inferred from imitation-centric planner training)
evidence_label.falsifiable_prediction: EXPECTED RESULT (pre-registered threshold; no measured numbers)
evidence_label.prior_work_basis: VERIFIED PRIOR WORK (well-known): execution-feedback self-training exists for code models; the procedural-scene visual variant is MODEL SPECULATION.

one_line_idea: Visual programs make failures locally attributable in a way chain-of-thought does not: automatic step-level attribution on synthetic scenes assigns blame to the true faulty step far above chance, enabling targeted fixes impossible for monolithic VLMs.
problem: The debuggability advantage claimed for visual programs has never been quantified: no one has measured whether, given a failure, the faulty step can actually be identified reliably and automatically.
core_hypothesis: Because each program step has a checkable input-output contract, automatic attribution (replay each step against synthetic-scene ground truth) localizes the true fault at rates far above the 1/steps chance baseline — and this localization accuracy is the measurable content of the paradigm's interpretability claim.
falsifiable_prediction: Automatic step-attribution accuracy reaches at least 70% on synthetic scenes with injected single-step faults, against a chance baseline near 1/steps. KILL: the claim dies if attribution accuracy is under 40% (debuggability claim hollow).
why_important: It converts 'interpretable' from a marketing adjective into a measured capability with direct payoff: attributable failures can be fixed component-wise, which monolithic VLM failures cannot.
why_possibly_novel: MODEL SPECULATION (unverified): interpretability claims for visual programs are common; a quantitative attribution-accuracy benchmark with injected faults may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Generate synthetic scenes with full state; run programs; inject single-step faults of known location; run the replay-based attributor; score localization accuracy against chance and against attribution from CoT text alone.
main_risk: Fault injection may create unrealistically clean single-fault cases; natural failures with correlated multi-step faults will be harder.
community_default_belief: Everyone already believes programs are more interpretable — measurement is unnecessary.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Belief without measurement has been wrong before in interpretability; and if attribution fails even on clean faults, the paradigm's central selling point needs revision.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One day, single GPU: 200 synthetic-scene failures with injected faults, attribution accuracy vs chance. Procedural data only.

evidence_label.community_default_belief: KNOWN FACT (interpretability is the standard motivation for visual programming)
evidence_label.falsifiable_prediction: EXPECTED RESULT (pre-registered threshold; no measured numbers)
evidence_label.prior_work_basis: MODEL SPECULATION: no verified quantitative attribution benchmark for visual programs.

one_line_idea: Annotation agents make correlated errors across seeds and prompt variants, so self-agreement massively overestimates label quality: unanimous agent labels stay wrong at rates that would be impossible for independent human annotators.
problem: Agent-annotation pipelines certify labels by agreement among multiple runs, borrowing the logic of inter-annotator agreement — but that logic assumes error independence, which repeated calls into the same model family do not provide.
core_hypothesis: Agent errors are systematically shared (same training data, same percepts), so the unanimity-implies-quality inference fails quantitatively: agreement among agent runs is nearly uninformative about correctness on the error-prone slice, unlike agreement among humans.
falsifiable_prediction: On a benchmark with trusted gold labels, the error rate among unanimous agent labels exceeds 10% on hard slices where human-unanimity error would be under 2%. KILL: the claim dies if unanimous-agent error is under 3% (agreement is trustworthy after all).
why_important: Datasets built with agreement-certified agent labels are entering training pipelines now; if unanimity is hollow, quality-control practice for machine-labeled data needs different foundations (cross-family ensembles, targeted human audit).
why_possibly_novel: MODEL SPECULATION (unverified): correlated LLM errors are discussed for text; a quantitative unanimity-vs-truth accounting for vision annotation agents may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run one annotation agent under 5 seeds and 3 prompt variants on a public labeled dataset treated as gold; compute error rates conditioned on agreement level; compare against human inter-annotator baselines where available.
main_risk: Gold labels have their own errors; disagreements between agents and gold need audit sampling to avoid mislabeling agent successes as failures.
community_default_belief: Agreement across multiple independent runs is evidence of label correctness, for machines as for humans.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Runs of the same model are not independent measurements; they are the same measurement repeated, and repeating a biased instrument does not remove its bias.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Half a day, single GPU: 1,000 items, 3 runs each, error-given-unanimity on the hard slice. Public data only.

evidence_label.community_default_belief: MODEL SPECULATION (inferred from agreement-based QC practice)
evidence_label.falsifiable_prediction: EXPECTED RESULT (pre-registered threshold; no measured numbers)
evidence_label.prior_work_basis: MODEL SPECULATION: correlated-error discussions exist for LLMs; vision-annotation unanimity accounting unverified.

one_line_idea: Cheap-proposer/expensive-verifier annotation cascades trace a predictable cost-quality frontier: verifying only flagged or disagreeing items achieves near full-expensive quality at a fraction of cost, and the frontier shape is estimable from a small pilot.
problem: Teams choose between cheap low-quality and expensive high-quality annotation models as a binary, lacking a quantitative design theory for cascades that spend expensive calls only where cheap calls are unreliable.
core_hypothesis: Disagreement and instability signals from the cheap tier identify most of its errors, so a cascade routing only that slice to the expensive tier sits near the expensive model's quality at a small fraction of its cost — and a 200-item pilot suffices to predict the full frontier before committing budget.
falsifiable_prediction: The cascade reaches at least 90% of the full-expensive quality gain over cheap-only while spending at most 40% of full-expensive cost, and pilot-predicted frontiers match realized frontiers within 10% cost. KILL: the claim dies if reaching 90% of the gain requires more than 70% of the cost.
why_important: Annotation is the dominant cost of dataset construction; a validated cascade calculus converts budget planning from guesswork into engineering for every lab building datasets with model labor.
why_possibly_novel: MODEL SPECULATION (unverified): model cascades are studied for inference; a pilot-predictable cost-quality frontier for annotation pipelines may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On a public labeled dataset, use a small open VLM as proposer and a larger open model as verifier; sweep routing thresholds to trace the realized frontier; fit the pilot predictor on 200 items and test its extrapolation.
main_risk: Cheap-tier errors that come with high self-consistency (correlated confident errors) evade routing and cap the cascade's ceiling.
community_default_belief: Label quality tracks the model you can afford to run on everything; partial verification is an unprincipled hack.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Errors are concentrated in a minority slice that cheap signals can flag; paying expert prices for the easy majority is the actual unprincipled choice.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One day, single GPU: two open models, 1,000 items, threshold sweep, pilot-vs-realized frontier check. Public data only.

evidence_label.community_default_belief: MODEL SPECULATION (inferred from single-tier annotation practice)
evidence_label.falsifiable_prediction: EXPECTED RESULT (pre-registered threshold; no measured numbers)
evidence_label.prior_work_basis: VERIFIED PRIOR WORK (well-known): inference cascades exist; annotation-frontier predictability is MODEL SPECULATION.

one_line_idea: Iterative self-labeling loops (train on agent labels, relabel with the trained model, retrain) amplify the agent's initial systematic biases at a measurable per-round rate rather than washing them out, producing datasets that look cleaner and are more biased each round.
problem: Self-labeling loops are deployed with the intuition that iteration denoises labels, but iteration also feeds the model its own biases as ground truth, and no one measures which force wins for visual annotation.
core_hypothesis: Random label noise shrinks across rounds while systematic bias compounds: any consistent initial tendency (boundary conventions, class confusions, attribute defaults) gets reinforced each cycle, so apparent quality (agreement, confidence) rises while distance from human ground truth on the biased dimensions grows.
falsifiable_prediction: A tracked bias metric grows by at least 20% per round for two or more rounds while inter-round agreement simultaneously rises. KILL: the claim dies if bias stays flat or decreases across rounds (iteration genuinely denoises).
why_important: Self-labeling is the scaling story for dataset construction; a bias-amplification law with a measurable rate would mandate anchor sets of human labels per round and bias-tracking as standard practice.
why_possibly_novel: MODEL SPECULATION (unverified): self-training drift is known in semi-supervised learning; a per-round bias-amplification rate for agentic visual annotation with the agreement-rises-too signature may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Seed a loop with an agent whose bias is measured against human labels on a public dataset; run 3 label-train-relabel rounds with an open model; track the bias metric and inter-round agreement per round.
main_risk: Compute for repeated retraining; small-model rounds may not represent large-model loop dynamics.
community_default_belief: Iterative pseudo-labeling is a denoising process; more rounds mean cleaner data.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Denoising theory assumes independent noise; systematic bias is signal to the retraining step, and signal gets amplified.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Two days, single GPU: small open model, 2 rounds on a public dataset subset, bias and agreement trajectories.

evidence_label.falsifiable_prediction: EXPECTED RESULT (pre-registered threshold; no measured numbers)
evidence_label.prior_work_basis: VERIFIED PRIOR WORK (well-known): self-training drift is documented in semi-supervised learning; the per-round amplification law for annotation agents is MODEL SPECULATION.

one_line_idea: Agent annotation is guideline-brittle: paraphrasing the annotation guidelines shifts label distributions by as much as swapping the underlying model, making 'the guideline' an unreported experimental variable in agent-built datasets.
problem: Datasets built by annotation agents report the model and the task but treat the guideline text as a fixed protocol, even though the agent's behavior is conditioned on that text token by token.
core_hypothesis: Semantically equivalent guideline paraphrases induce label-distribution shifts comparable in magnitude to changing the annotation model itself, concentrated on boundary cases — meaning dataset reproducibility requires publishing and versioning exact guideline text as a first-class artifact.
falsifiable_prediction: Across 5 meaning-preserving guideline paraphrases, the induced label-distribution shift is at least 25% of the shift induced by swapping between two open annotation models. KILL: the claim dies if the paraphrase effect is under 25% of the model-swap effect (guidelines are robust).
why_important: If guidelines are as causally potent as models, dataset cards, replication studies, and downstream comparisons are all missing a variable that changes their conclusions.
why_possibly_novel: MODEL SPECULATION (unverified): prompt sensitivity is generic knowledge; quantifying guideline-paraphrase variance against a model-swap yardstick for visual annotation may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Write 5 paraphrases of one guideline validated as equivalent by independent readers; annotate a fixed public image set under all paraphrases and two models; compare shift magnitudes on matched items.
main_risk: Paraphrase equivalence is contestable; leakage of substantive changes into paraphrases would inflate the effect.
community_default_belief: The guideline states the task; reasonable rewordings of the same rules yield the same labels.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Agents do not read rules the way trained annotators do — every phrasing choice shifts the conditional distribution the agent samples from, especially at category boundaries.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Half a day, single GPU: 500 items, 3 paraphrases, 2 open models, shift comparison. Public data only.

evidence_label.falsifiable_prediction: EXPECTED RESULT (pre-registered threshold; no measured numbers)
evidence_label.prior_work_basis: MODEL SPECULATION: prompt sensitivity is well known; guideline-vs-model effect-size comparison for annotation unverified.

one_line_idea: Annotation agents allowed to request extra evidence (zoomed crops, alternate frames) on self-flagged hard instances beat fixed-pipeline agents at matched cost, because evidence acquisition — not model quality — limits label accuracy on the hard tail.
problem: Annotation pipelines process every item through the same fixed views, spending identical evidence budgets on trivial and borderline instances alike, while the error mass concentrates in the borderline slice that needed one more look.
core_hypothesis: The hard tail of annotation error is evidence-limited: giving the agent an evidence-request action (zoom, adjacent frame, enhanced view) with a budget reallocated from the easy majority cuts tail error more than upgrading the annotation model at the same total cost.
falsifiable_prediction: The active-evidence agent cuts hard-tail error by at least 20% relative at matched total cost, beating a model-upgrade control. KILL: the claim dies if tail-error reduction is under 5% or the bigger model dominates at equal cost.
why_important: It reframes annotation quality as an acquisition problem rather than purely a model problem, with a mechanism any pipeline can add — and budget accounting that makes the comparison honest.
why_possibly_novel: MODEL SPECULATION (unverified): active learning selects which items to label; agent-initiated evidence acquisition per item inside annotation loops may be largely untested.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On public datasets with hard-case stratification, run fixed vs active-evidence agents at equal total inference cost (charging evidence requests), plus a larger-model control; compare tail and overall error.
main_risk: Self-flagging may miss the truly hard cases (the agent does not know what it does not know), capping the mechanism's reach.
community_default_belief: Annotation accuracy is a property of the model; pipelines are plumbing that should stay simple and uniform.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Humans given one fixed view would also fail the borderline cases; experts zoom — the capability gap is in the loop's acquisition policy, not only in the model.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One day, single GPU: 500 items with hard slice, both agents at matched cost, tail-error comparison. Public data only.

evidence_label.falsifiable_prediction: EXPECTED RESULT (pre-registered threshold; no measured numbers)
evidence_label.prior_work_basis: VERIFIED PRIOR WORK (well-known): active learning exists at item-selection level; per-item evidence acquisition in annotation loops is MODEL SPECULATION.

one_line_idea: Agent annotators erode dataset tails: rare classes are systematically relabeled toward frequent ones, so agent-curated datasets measurably shrink tail mass each generation, with compounding effects on models trained downstream.
problem: Agent relabeling and cleaning passes are applied to existing datasets to fix noisy labels, but the agent's priors reflect the head of its training distribution, making rare-class instances look like errors to be corrected.
core_hypothesis: Tail erosion is directional and systematic: confusion between a rare and a frequent class is resolved toward the frequent class far more often than chance, so each agent pass transfers probability mass from tail to head, and models trained on eroded data erode future passes further.
falsifiable_prediction: One agent relabeling pass reduces tail-class mass by at least 15% relative, with rare-to-frequent flips outnumbering frequent-to-rare flips by at least 3:1. KILL: the claim dies if tail mass changes by under 3% or flips are direction-balanced.
why_important: Long-tail performance is already the weak point of vision systems; if the data pipeline itself eats tails, the field is quietly destroying exactly the data it most needs, and tail-protection rules become mandatory for agent curation.
why_possibly_novel: MODEL SPECULATION (unverified): label-noise cleaning side effects are discussed; a directional tail-erosion accounting for agent relabeling with flip-asymmetry ratios may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Run an open VLM relabeling pass over a public long-tailed classification dataset; measure per-class mass changes and the flip-direction matrix; repeat with a second model family for robustness.
main_risk: Some tail relabels are genuine error corrections; audit sampling of flipped items is required to separate erosion from cleaning.
community_default_belief: Model-assisted relabeling cleans datasets; disagreements with existing labels are mostly caught errors.
why_it_might_be_wrong: For a prior-driven annotator, a rare class is statistically indistinguishable from a labeling mistake — so it fixes the dataset by deleting reality's tail.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Half a day, single GPU: relabel a long-tailed public subset, flip-direction matrix plus audit of 100 flips. Public data only.

evidence_label.falsifiable_prediction: EXPECTED RESULT (pre-registered threshold; no measured numbers)
evidence_label.prior_work_basis: MODEL SPECULATION: label-cleaning literature exists; directional tail-erosion accounting unverified.

one_line_idea: Label provenance is recoverable: a classifier can distinguish models trained on agent-labeled versus human-labeled data using only behavioral probes, enabling post-hoc audits of dataset supply chains.
problem: As agent-labeled data floods training pipelines, there is no way to audit after the fact whether a model's training labels were machine-generated — a growing provenance question for accountability, licensing, and scientific reporting.
core_hypothesis: Agent labels carry systematic signatures (boundary conventions, confusion structure, tail treatment, round-number artifacts) that persist through training into model behavior, so a probe suite over a trained model separates agent-labeled from human-labeled training provenance without accessing the training data.
falsifiable_prediction: A provenance classifier over behavioral probes achieves at least 0.75 AUC on held-out model pairs trained on matched images with agent vs human labels. KILL: the claim dies if AUC is 0.6 or below (signatures do not survive training).
why_important: Provenance auditing is infrastructure the field will need for dataset governance, contamination studies, and the recursive-training question of models learning from model outputs.
why_possibly_novel: MODEL SPECULATION (unverified): membership inference and dataset inference exist; label-provenance inference from behavioral signatures may be a new problem formulation.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Train matched small models on a public dataset under its human labels vs agent-generated labels (several seeds each); build behavioral probes (boundary cases, confusion asymmetries, tail behavior); train and evaluate the provenance classifier across held-out pairs.
main_risk: Signatures may be architecture- or dataset-specific, failing to generalize across training setups the auditor does not control.
community_default_belief: Once training is done, the origin of the labels is unrecoverable from the model; labels are interchangeable supervision.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Training is compression, and systematic label conventions are exactly the kind of regularity compression preserves.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Two days, single GPU: two small models (agent vs human labels) on one public dataset, probe suite, held-out AUC.

evidence_label.falsifiable_prediction: EXPECTED RESULT (pre-registered threshold; no measured numbers)
evidence_label.prior_work_basis: VERIFIED PRIOR WORK (well-known): membership/dataset inference exist; label-provenance inference is MODEL SPECULATION.

one_line_idea: Cross-seed disagreement among annotation agents is a cheap detector of genuinely ambiguous instances: agent disagreement predicts human inter-annotator disagreement well enough to route only truly ambiguous items to humans.
problem: Pipelines need to separate 'the agent is unreliable here' from 'humans would also disagree here', because the first needs a better model and the second needs an adjudication protocol — but both look identical as low agreement.
core_hypothesis: After controlling for instance difficulty to the agent (via evidence manipulations that fix agent-side failures), residual cross-seed disagreement tracks genuine task ambiguity, correlating with human inter-annotator disagreement strongly enough to serve as a router.
falsifiable_prediction: Agent-disagreement scores correlate with human disagreement at Spearman rho of at least 0.5 on datasets with multi-annotator labels. KILL: the claim dies if rho is under 0.25 (agent disagreement is mostly agent noise).
why_important: A validated ambiguity router lets datasets record ambiguity as signal (label distributions) instead of forcing false consensus — and spends human adjudication exactly where humans are needed.
why_possibly_novel: MODEL SPECULATION (unverified): model disagreement is used for uncertainty-style sampling in active learning; validating it against human disagreement as an ambiguity meter for annotation routing may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: On public multi-annotator datasets, compute cross-seed agent disagreement per item; correlate with human answer entropy; test routing utility by measuring adjudication yield on high-disagreement slices.
main_risk: The correlation may be driven by a shared covariate (image quality) rather than ambiguity per se; needs the evidence-manipulation control.
community_default_belief: Agent disagreement means the agent is weak; ambiguity detection needs humans.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Ambiguity is a property of the instance-task pair that any competent annotator population, human or machine, will express as disagreement.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Half a day, single GPU: 500 multi-annotator items, 5 agent seeds, correlation test. Public data only.

evidence_label.community_default_belief: MODEL SPECULATION (inferred from weak-model framing of disagreement)
evidence_label.falsifiable_prediction: EXPECTED RESULT (pre-registered threshold; no measured numbers)
evidence_label.prior_work_basis: VERIFIED PRIOR WORK (well-known): disagreement-based sampling exists in active learning; human-ambiguity validation for routing is MODEL SPECULATION.

one_line_idea: Compiling natural-language annotation guidelines into executable checklists (ordered binary probes with evidence requirements) improves agent label consistency more than upgrading the base model, because guideline interpretation is the dominant noise source.
problem: Guidelines are written as prose humans internalize through training sessions, but agents re-interpret the prose on every item, injecting interpretation variance that looks like model weakness.
core_hypothesis: Most inter-run label inconsistency traces to unstable guideline interpretation rather than unstable perception; compiling prose into a fixed decision procedure (ordered binary questions, each with an evidence rule) removes the interpretation step and cuts variance more than a model-class upgrade does.
falsifiable_prediction: Checklist compilation reduces cross-run label variance by at least 30% relative, exceeding the variance reduction from a one-class model upgrade under prose guidelines. KILL: the claim dies if variance reduction is under 10% or the model upgrade dominates.
why_important: It relocates annotation-quality engineering from model procurement to guideline compilation — a one-time cost per task that any team can pay, and a transferable artifact unlike prompt magic.
why_possibly_novel: MODEL SPECULATION (unverified): decision-tree protocols exist in human annotation practice; measuring compiled-checklist gains against model-upgrade gains for agent annotators may be new.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Compile two public dataset guidelines into checklists; run prose vs checklist conditions across seeds and two model classes; decompose label variance into interpretation vs perception components via evidence-fixed controls.
main_risk: Checklists can encode the compiler's reading errors permanently, trading variance for bias; bias against gold labels must be tracked alongside variance.
community_default_belief: Label consistency comes from better models and lower temperature; guidelines are content, not architecture.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Humans get calibration sessions precisely because prose under-determines edge cases; agents get no sessions, so the prose's slack becomes per-item noise.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One day, single GPU: one guideline compiled, 500 items, variance comparison across 5 seeds and two conditions. Public data only.

evidence_label.falsifiable_prediction: EXPECTED RESULT (pre-registered threshold; no measured numbers)
evidence_label.prior_work_basis: MODEL SPECULATION: human decision-tree protocols exist; agent-side compilation accounting unverified.

one_line_idea: Given a fixed human budget inside an agent annotation loop, spending it on adjudicating agent disagreements dominates spending it on random spot-checks or gold seeding, and the advantage concentrates exactly where datasets matter most — the ambiguous tail.
problem: Human effort inside machine-annotation loops is allocated by convention (random QA samples, upfront gold sets) without ever comparing allocation strategies at equal budget for final dataset quality.
core_hypothesis: Human labels are most valuable where agents disagree, because that slice concentrates both agent errors and genuine ambiguity; adjudication allocation therefore yields lower final error than random spot-checking (which mostly audits easy correct labels) or upfront gold seeding (which spends before knowing where help is needed).
falsifiable_prediction: At equal human budget, adjudication allocation yields at least 15% lower final dataset error than random spot-checking. KILL: the claim dies if the advantage is 5% or less, or if gold seeding wins (calibration beats correction).
why_important: Every hybrid pipeline makes this allocation decision implicitly; an empirical dominance result converts it into a defensible default with direct quality-per-dollar impact.
why_possibly_novel: MODEL SPECULATION (unverified): active-learning theory addresses which items to label for training; allocation of human labor across roles inside annotation loops (adjudicate vs audit vs seed) may be unstudied.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Simulate the three allocations on public multi-annotator datasets using held-out human labels as the human budget; measure final dataset error against full-human reference at three budget levels.
main_risk: Simulation with existing labels may not capture real adjudicator behavior on items agents flag; a small live-annotation replication strengthens it.
community_default_belief: Random QA sampling is the honest way to spend human effort; targeting is biased.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Random sampling optimizes unbiased quality estimation, not quality itself; if the goal is a better dataset rather than a better estimate, targeting the disagreement slice is the correct objective.
fastest_falsification_experiment: Half a day, CPU/single GPU: simulation over 2 public multi-annotator datasets, three allocations, one budget level.

evidence_label.falsifiable_prediction: EXPECTED RESULT (pre-registered threshold; no measured numbers)
evidence_label.prior_work_basis: VERIFIED PRIOR WORK (well-known): active learning theory exists for item selection; role-allocation comparison inside annotation loops is MODEL SPECULATION.

family_fingerprint.manipulated_variable: human-labor placement (adjudicate vs audit vs seed)
family_fingerprint.measurement_family: final dataset error at matched budget

one_line_idea: LLM-guided where-to-look policies barely beat brute-force grid scanning at matched crop budgets: most of the reported benefit of visual-search agents comes from having more pixels, not from intelligent search.
problem: Visual-search agents are credited with intelligent question-driven exploration, but their evaluations rarely include the dumb control that spends the identical crop budget on a uniform grid.
core_hypothesis: The dominant term in visual-search gains is resolution recovery (any policy that inspects more pixels wins over a single downscaled pass); the search policy's contribution on top of budget is small except in extreme needle-in-haystack regimes.
falsifiable_prediction: At matched crop budgets, guided search beats grid scanning by under 2 points on standard small-object VQA, with a larger margin only when targets occupy under 0.1% of image area. KILL: the claim dies if guided search beats matched-budget grids by 5+ points on standard benchmarks.
why_important: If budget, not intelligence, drives the numbers, the engineering conclusion flips: build cheap wide scanning with good aggregation instead of expensive LLM-planned search.
why_possibly_novel: MODEL SPECULATION (unverified): visual-search agents publish against no-search baselines; matched-budget grid controls with target-size stratification may be systematically missing.
minimal_falsification_experiment: Reimplement one open visual-search loop; add a grid-scan control at exactly matched crop count and resolution; evaluate both on public small-object benchmarks stratified by relative target size.
main_risk: Grid aggregation quality (how crops' answers combine) confounds the control; both arms must share the aggregation mechanism.
community_default_belief: Question-guided visual search is intelligent exploration and the source of the accuracy gains.
why_it_might_be_wrong: Most benchmark targets are findable by any policy that looks everywhere at adequate resolution; guidance only matters when looking everywhere is infeasible.
fastest_falsification_experiment: One day, single GPU: one search loop vs matched grid on 300 stratified instances. Public data only.

evidence_label.falsifiable_prediction: EXPECTED RESULT (pre-registered threshold; no measured numbers)
evidence_label.prior_work_basis: VERIFIED PRIOR WORK (well-known): guided visual-search agents exist; the matched-budget attribution claim is MODEL SPECULATION.

family_fingerprint.manipulated_variable: search policy at matched crop budget
family_fingerprint.measurement_family: accuracy attribution between policy and budget

one_line_idea: Agent fixations track bottom-up saliency, not the question: look-location distributions barely shift across different questions about the same image, revealing that 'question-guided' viewing in current loops is mostly generic salience.
problem: Zoom agents claim question-conditioned attention, but if the same regions get inspected regardless of what is asked, the question is decoration and the loop is a saliency scanner with extra cost.
core_hypothesis: The question's causal effect on look locations is weak: across-question variation in fixation distributions for a fixed image is a small fraction of across-image variation, and the fixations correlate better with generic saliency than with question-relevant ground-truth regions.
